#10096. Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver

I help lead Google's agent skills program, currently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills. To keep that many skill files consistent, I wrote skill-lint, a standalone Go CLI that checks SKILL.md files and applies LLM-generated line edits before they ship. Even with skill-lint's own unit and fuzz test suite, a small slice or line-number mistake inside its Markdown parsers or edit applier can sit dormant until an unusual file or edit range triggers a runtime panic in the linter.

In Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out. To hunt for crashes, I compiled key functions from my code to see which panic traps survived optimization, and Gemini 4 Argon translated the path to each trap into rules for the Z3 constraint solver. An LLM-written solver model isn't a sound proof system, but it gives the agent an independent way to reason about control flow and synthesize concrete Go reproducers, and every crash it finds is real because go test runs the offending bytes directly. That workflow caught all three bugs I planted in test parsers and turned up three latent bugs in skill-lint.

In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.

A recent post from Anthropic showed how formal verification catches latent bugs in C and C++ by having frontier AI models write machine-checked Rocq proofs across OSS-Fuzz libraries. Instead of sampling random inputs like a fuzzer, a formal tool works backward from each failure condition to solve for the exact input that triggers it. Full theorem proving is still too heavy for most day-to-day Go projects, so I wanted to see how much of that bug-hunting power an agent can get from an LLM and a constraint solver in about a minute per function.

In C and C++, reading or writing past the end of a buffer corrupts memory. Go catches out-of-bounds access at runtime instead, compiling every slice or index operation it can't prove safe into an explicit branch to runtime.panicBounds that panics, crashing the process unless recovered.

Before generating machine code, Go's SSA prove pass already eliminates most of those checks by tracking slice lengths and loop variables. That optimization pass leaves behind only the runtime.panicBounds traps the compiler couldn't rule out on its own, giving the solver a short list of candidate crash sites to target.

I compiled each target with GOOS=linux GOARCH=riscv64 go build -gcflags="-S -d=ssa/check_bce/debug=1" (-S prints the assembly listing and ssa/check_bce/debug=1 logs every surviving bounds check) and passed both the Go source and the disassembly to the model. Looking at Go source alone, you can't see which bounds checks the compiler already removed or where a register gets truncated to 8 bits; in the disassembly, both show up. I targeted RISC-V because it's the instruction set Anthropic's post targets for its Rocq proofs, and Go cross-compiles to it out of the box.

From there, Argon read the Go source and disassembly and returned a Z3 script modeling the path to each surviving trap, along with a patched function whenever it flagged a bug. Z3 then checked whether those constraints could be satisfied, and whenever it found a crashing input, go test replayed those bytes against the real function. Using an LLM saved me from translating assembly into solver constraints by hand. Argon's translation dominated the runtime, at about a minute per function, while Z3 itself finished in milliseconds.

Anthropic's approach relies on interactive theorem proving, where experts model machine semantics and Rocq checks LLM-generated proofs against those rules. In contrast, my workflow uses a constraint solver based on satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), relying on Argon to translate assembly directly into Z3 constraints. While a constraint solver doesn't provide a complete correctness proof without a semantic model, it is highly effective for finding bugs. Z3's check-sat command returns sat when input constraints can be satisfied and unsat when they cannot.

A sat answer ("definitely buggy") comes with concrete bytes aimed at the trap, and go test runs them against the real function. Once go test panics, you have a concrete bug reproducer regardless of whether Argon's model was sound. Like a Bloom filter for bugs, an unsat answer only means "maybe correct." Trading away a correctness proof is what makes the approach so practical: you get most of the bug-finding value of formal methods for a tiny fraction of the effort.

Anthropic's setup proved no-crash properties on whole binaries under a 64 MB budget; I checked individual functions on fresh 64-byte slices where cap(buf) == len(buf), so any slice past len(buf) panics. (If you want the full-binary Rocq setup for Go, theorem-labs/oss-verify includes a Go 1.27 runtime overlay that makes the runtime single-threaded and deterministic.)

For the fuzzing baseline, I ran unseeded go test -fuzz on Go 1.27.3 against each planted bug: one 3-second run and three 60-second runs, each with a fresh fuzz cache so a short time budget wouldn't explain a miss.

I started with three safe parsers to make sure the pipeline didn't flag clean code. The compiler's prove pass removed every bounds check in a TOML key parser on its own, and Z3 returned unsat on the remaining traps in an HTTP header scanner and a varint decoder.

Then I wrote three parsers with subtle panics. Here's the first one, ParseTwoChunkFrame:

In the RISC-V disassembly, the bug is much easier to see:

total := hdrLen + bodyLen adds two uint8 values, so MOVBU wraps the sum at 256 before the length guard checks it, while endBody adds the full 64-bit ints. Argon turned those instructions into a Z3 query asking whether a fresh slice of up to 64 bytes can pass the guard and still fail the endBody check at 0x0092:

Z3 returned a 59-byte counterexample with hdrLen = 48 and bodyLen = 236: their uint8 sum wraps from 284 down to 28 (so 28 + 4 ≤ 59 passes the guard), and buf[endHdr:endBody] then slices to index 288 and panics.

At 59 bytes, 19.4% of all possible (hdrLen, bodyLen) pairs trigger this crash. Yet a 3-second fuzz run missed it, and so did three 60-second runs.

Go checks a slice expression like buf[endHdr:endBody] against the slice's capacity, not its length, and Go's fuzzer rarely passes a slice without spare capacity. In a 10-second probe of 386,741 fuzz calls, 89% of inputs were views into a shared ~100 MB buffer, and only 0.07% had cap == len. With that much spare capacity, endBody (at most 514) never exceeds cap(buf), so the buggy parser returns bytes past the end of buf instead of panicking.

The second target, ExtractQuotedToken, hit the same blind spot when a trailing backslash pushed the index one byte past len(buf). Z3 caught it immediately with the 2-byte input []byte{'"', '\\'}, while the fuzzer absorbed the overrun in spare capacity.

Clipping capacity to length with a full slice expression turns any slice past len into a panic:

After that change, the fuzzer crashed both ParseTwoChunkFrame and ExtractQuotedToken in all three runs (median 0.28 s and 0.17 s). The third target, ParseMagicPacket, was a control because its signed int8 length bug panics on a negative index regardless of capacity, and the fuzzer found it in every run either way. Fuzzing still can't give you an unsat signal across the remaining paths, which is how I checked the three safe parsers and Argon's patches.

Next, I pointed the pipeline at skill-lint itself. A whole Go CLI is too large to hand to a solver directly. Even a 10-line parser links 1,559 symbols from the Go runtime, and the 28 MB skill-lint binary has 32,321 symbols in total. Following Functional Core, Imperative Shell, I left CLI flags, network calls, and file I/O to go test -fuzz and go test -race, and ran the solver only on pure functions and slice helpers extracted from file-reading code.

Of the five functions I tested, two scanners came back unsat (including a CRLF line splitter with six surviving bounds checks), and the other three had bugs. The sharpest was in ApplyReplacementChunks, which validates LLM-generated {StartLine, EndLine} edits against the initial line count and sorts them bottom-to-top so earlier edits don't shift later line numbers:

Z3 immediately returned sat because sorting by StartLine doesn't prevent two chunks from overlapping. In the extracted helper, which checks bounds once up front, replacing lines 3 and 4 of a 4-line file with one line shrinks lines to 3 elements, so a second chunk spanning lines 2 through 4 evaluates lines[4:] and panics with slice bounds out of range [4:3]. In the shipped ApplyChunks, a per-iteration bounds check turns that case into a misleading range error, while overlapping chunks that stay within len(lines) silently overwrite the earlier edit. Rejecting overlapping chunks after the sort fixes both.

The other two bugs were similar accounting errors. In the local fixer, target line numbers were checked once per violation before the inner chunk loop applied deletions that shrank the slice (a latent panic if a fixer ever returns a second chunk after a deletion, though DeleteLineFix only returns one today). In the prompt packer, a truncation check reserved a flat 100 bytes for a ~70-byte wrapper plus file path, overshooting the 2 MB context budget in the shipped code when a path exceeds about 30 bytes and panicking in the extracted helper.

When you check a function modularly like this, the target has to include its own entry-point guards (like the bounds check and sort in ApplyReplacementChunks). If an internal helper assumes preconditions that are only enforced by its caller or stated in a doc comment, Z3 will happily invent inputs that violate them. Because each extracted helper included its entry guards, false positives weren't an issue: across all six buggy functions in my tests, the first sat assignment Z3 returned triggered a real panic in go test without needing to filter out non-crashing candidates or loop back into the solver.

Once I pulled these helpers away from file I/O, a 3-second fuzz run caught all three bugs too. To make sure Argon wasn't leaning on source comments in my test files, I also reran the skill-lint targets with all comments stripped; Argon and Z3 still caught all three bugs and returned unsat on the two scanners and all three patches.

Staying entirely inside the target language makes a whole class of bugs hard for an agent to see. When an LLM reviews Go source directly, a line like if int(total)+4 > len(buf) looks like a textbook bounds check, and when it runs go test -fuzz, target-language runtime details like spare slice capacity or multi-step precondition checks can hide the crash indefinitely. Asking the agent to translate Go and assembly into a constraint solver forces a change of representation that strips away surface syntax and makes every bit width and slice bound explicit, while go test turns any solver hit back into a concrete Go reproducer.

For most Go code, fuzzing pure helpers with slice capacity clipped to length will catch bounds bugs in seconds. A solver is worth the extra minute on the traps that survive both the compiler's range prover and a quick fuzz run, especially in parsers and editors that compute offsets from multi-field headers or line ranges.

Single-threaded solver models don't see data races or deadlocks, so concurrent code still belongs with the race detector, deterministic concurrency testing, and Go 1.27's goroutine leak profiles.

If you're experimenting with solvers or coding agents on Go, let's compare notes on X or LinkedIn.

#10095. 🤗 Kernels: Major Updates

In our previous post (From Zero to GPU), we introduced the 🤗 Kernels project, which aims at standardizing how custom kernels are packaged, distributed, and consumed. We want the project to be frictionless and secure, while making it as Hub-friendly as possible.

Over the past few months, we have worked towards this goal. In the process, we also almost completely redesigned the project. This post will summarize the major updates we have shipped and what’s coming.

We have introduced a new repository type on the Hub called "kernel". This enables us to cater to users with compute-related specificities. For example, a user can get a sense of which accelerators, operating systems, and backend versions are supported for a given kernel:

One can browse all available kernels on the Hub here: https://huggingface.co/kernels.

Making these kernels first-class citizens of the Hub also benefits the AI ecosystem. Users can now see trends across kernels, models, and the applications that use them. The kernels become more discoverable to users.

Kernels run native code with the same privileges as the Python process that loads them, so a malicious kernel can do real harm. Therefore, security has always been of utmost importance to the Kernels project.

This is why we focused early on reproducibility: you should be able to recompile a kernel yourself and verify that it matches the publicly available source. We use Nix to make this possible, since it keeps builds pure through hermetic evaluation of the build recipe and a strongly isolated sandbox. We further improve provenance by embedding the source Git SHA1 into the kernel itself.

In recent months, we have added additional layers of defense: trusted kernel publishers and code signing.

With the new repo type, we also introduced “trusted publishers”. Since kernels execute code on a machine with the same privileges as the Python process they are used in, an attacker could compromise machines by uploading a malicious kernel and coaxing you to use that kernel. To help you avoid such malicious kernels, the kernels package will now only load kernels by trusted publishers by default. A trusted publisher is an organization that is trusted by the community to act in good faith.

We still want to support loading kernels from organizations or users that are not trusted publishers, but you have to explicitly opt in using the trust_remote_code argument when loading a kernel from the Hub:

By default, users cannot publish kernel repositories on the Hub. They have to request to be a kernel publisher. Users and organizations can request for access from their account settings. This gives us time to treat these requests on a case-by-case basis.

An additional layer of security that we are adding is code signing. Code signing protects against the scenario where an attacker uploads a malicious kernel to a kernel repo from a trusted publisher whose Hub credentials were compromised. In code signing, a kernel is signed with a private key known only to the kernel developer and validated with a public key that is generally available. In the Hub compromise scenario, an attacker cannot sign the malicious kernel since they do not own the private key needed for signing.

To further improve security, we use Sigstore’s cosign to sign using ephemeral private keys. Since these signing keys are only valid for a limited time, an attacker typically cannot use the private key, even when it is leaked. We also verify that the kernel was signed by a trusted GitHub workflow from a trusted GitHub repository.

Kernel signing is already supported by kernel-builder and we have provided the kernels verify-signature to verify a kernel. Kernels does not verify the signature upon loading a kernel yet, since we would like to test this new functionality more before fully rolling it out. Preliminary notes on setting up code signing for your own kernels can be found in the kernels 0.16.0 release notes: https://github.com/huggingface/kernels/releases/tag/v0.16.0.

Previously, a bunch of utilities were intertwined between kernels and kernel-builder. We have established a better separation of concern between the CLI of kernels and kernel-builder. The mental model here is that kernels is a library for loading and preparing kernels for use. Therefore, it should not include anything related to “building” kernels.

As a result of this, both kernels and kernel-builder are now much leaner and more specific. Refer to the documentation to learn more about this:

This improved CLI experience also lets us cater to the rise of agentic kernel development in a better manner. More on this later.

We have extended support for frameworks, the most visible changes are:

kernel-builder and kernels complement the rise of agentic kernel development wherein an agent is leveraged to come up with an (optimized) kernel from scratch. Together, they support a workflow in which agents can scaffold, build, benchmark, and iteratively optimize kernels.

Agentic kernel development is still nascent, and the right development loops will continue to evolve. That makes simple, clear fundamentals especially important where the tools should be easy to compose into whichever agent workflows or frameworks people choose to use.

kernel-builder helps enforce a structure in how kernel source code should be scaffolded and used to perform reproducible builds. This gives agents a predictable project layout and repeatable workflow to operate within. Its CLI is also meant to be agent-optimized. For example, this can mean non-interactive commands and outputs that are straightforward for an agent to interpret programmatically. To this end, we also have backend-specific skills to help agents navigate the idiosyncrasies of different backends. These skills can capture backend-specific toolchains, compilation paths, and performance considerations.

Building a kernel successfully isn’t the only goal, we need to ensure that it delivers actual speedups over a baseline on the target hardware. A successful build is therefore only the first validation step. Usually, this target hardware can include many different accelerators, even different families of the same accelerator.

This makes it important to evaluate results across hardware vendors and generations where relevant. Our tight integration with HF Jobs can make this benchmarking process easy. Agents can use this integration to run benchmark suites, collect performance results, and compare them against a defined baseline.

This way, agents can run tests across different hardware configurations to get reliable feedback on the performance of the generated kernels and identify what needs to be done. That feedback can then inform the next optimization iteration.

Below are some examples of agent-augmented kernels. These illustrate the kinds of kernels that can be developed and evaluated through this workflow:

The environment setup for building kernels with kernel-builder can be daunting. To make it easier for users, we now have an installation script for setting up an environment in one click. If you prefer working with ephemeral instances, our Terraform setup guide is worth following.

After the kernels are built, we create a system card for each kernel to expose useful information, including how to use it and its exposed interfaces. When the kernel is pushed to the Hub, this system card becomes the front matter for the kernel:

Is a question one would ask multiple times to plan things better. Use the has_kernel() method for this purpose:

It returns a bool. If you’re looking for more explanations around why a given kernel isn’t supported then use get_kernel_variants():

It should print (depends on the machine you’re on):

Kernel-builder has targeted manylinux_2_28 almost since the beginning. We used to target manylinux by using a modern gcc toolchain compiled with glibc 2.28. To avoid compatibility issues with older versions of libstdc++, we statically linked libstdc++.

However, this approach recently resulted in some issues. Some libstdc++ functionality uses global initialization. This can lead to corrupted data when multiple libstdc++ versions come into play, such as the libstdc++ that is linked dynamically by PyTorch and the libstdc++ that is linked statically by a kernel. Some recent kernels use functionality (e.g. C++ regexes) that trigger global initializations, leading to such corrupted data, causing segfaults and other issues.

To solve this issue, kernels now link libstdc++ dynamically. To ensure compatibility with old libstdc++ versions, we now compile kernels with the official manylinux_2_28 toolchain.

Our goal with the Kernels project is to serve both kernel developers and users of custom kernels. We’re always keen on receiving feedback from the community on how we can improve it. Don’t hesitate to contribute!

Acknowledgements: Thanks to Aritra for reviewing the post.

Louis Erbkamm built the first prototype in his free time. Now GitHub Copilot helps him maintain it alone.

Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it.

I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet.

Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors.

Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school.

That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow.

Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with.

The project didn’t have a name yet, so it borrowed the town’s unique moniker.

When Arnis added elevation, its worlds stopped being flat, and geospatial specialists from all over showed up with ideas on how best to integrate it. They started discussions on their own, and Louis says that’s exactly what he needed.

Bigger calls happen in the open too: before porting Arnis from Python to Rust, Louis opened discussions on GitHub to hear different perspectives. Contributors have since translated Arnis into about 20 languages and built major features of their own.

The best thing that has happened to me is essentially this big community on GitHub to see actually people from all kinds of different fields coming together to work on something that I started as a side project.

Some features start on a walk. Louis noticed how many trash bins there were in his city, and there were none in his generated worlds.

Minecraft has no dedicated bins, so he took the question to the community, and together they found a block that fit. Placing one follows the same path as everything else: for the area a user selects, Arnis queries OpenStreetMap for every mapped element, then looks up each element’s coordinates and type.

If an element isn’t mapped, Arnis can’t place it. For structures too detailed for the map to describe, like the Statue of Liberty in New York, or Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Arnis converts 3D models into Minecraft blocks.

As the sole maintainer, Louis reviews every pull request himself, and they stack up. He usually spends evenings or weekends working on Arnis, which means the community has to wait for him to be done with work for the day.

He uses GitHub Copilot to get an overview of open issues and bugs from the latest release, see how many people are running into them, trace where a bug came from in the codebase, and create a fix. Since he brought AI into the project, he says, code reviews and documentation have both increased.

I could delegate those annoying and boring tasks to Copilot, while I could still have a look at those really cool topics that are related to the development of it.

Big features arrive as big pull requests.

Louis opens a large pull request in the GitHub Copilot app for a first overview and a performance review, with Copilot running in the background looking for small changes that would cut memory usage or generation time.

It takes just one wrong calculation in street lights, for example, to make the generation time of an entire city much slower.

He also keeps a mental list of the areas of the codebase that need extra care whenever someone changes them, and he has written the same warnings out by hand over and over.

I’m starting a few sub agents with the GitHub Copilot app to have a look specifically at those cases, and to come up with corner cases to test to make sure that we do not introduce any regressions into new releases.

He likes that the terminal, his files, the code changes and the pull request all sit in one app next to the chat.

Louis’s favorite use of Arnis is in schools, where teachers have generated their city or a neighborhood park.

Some turn it into a contest: every student starts from the same generated area, improves a nearby park or playground using Arnis and Minecraft, and the class looks at the results together.

Recent releases have gone beyond the bounds of Earth, adding the Moon and Mars. Louis wants Arnis to stay easy to use while getting closer to reality, with more detail in less time, and he would like to see it in more schools.

Download Arnis from github.com/louis-e/arnis, pick a place on the map, choose where to spawn, and click Start Generation: within a few minutes, the world is ready to open in Minecraft. Louis suggests a place you know, like your hometown or somewhere memorable you’ve been, such as the Grand Canyon or Niagara Falls. Then look for what’s missing.

So maybe you see a bench that was not generated even though it is there.

Map it on OpenStreetMap, or tell Louis if it’s a bug and he will fix it.

Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.

#10092. Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime

New regulator will require modelmakers to test and allow inspection, but not much more

Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models.

Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks.

Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI.

That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.”

Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.”

The review suggests two ministries and Australia’s Federal Police consider those reforms, meaning this is not something that will happen in a hurry, if at all, for a couple of reasons.

One is that Australia yesterday proposed a new regulator which will require AI players to do six things:

Maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment

Identify and manage serious risks associated with their models

Allow independent evaluation of their models

Provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian Government rapidly

Maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency

Respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

If AI companies straighten up and fly right, Canberra might not need to do more.

The other reason Australia might not criminalize AI is economic pragmatism.

Canberra wants to ensure leading AI companies invest in local datacenters, especially facilities where they train and run frontier models. Such investments would mean Australia scores some of the AI boom cash sloshing around the world, while also giving the government the ability to at least point to leading-edge AI running on local shores and therefore theoretically remaining accessible even if war or a diplomatic rupture makes it hard to access advanced AI hosted offshore.

Other nations in Asia, such as South Korea and India, are addressing those risks by building substantial sovereign infrastructure and working to develop sovereign frontier-class models trained on local data and especially data in their local languages.

Canberra can’t match that investment without pouring petrol on its raging inflation problem. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is therefore instead trying to regulate AI without scaring away investment.

Threatening to lock up AI executives is not likely to make them enthusiastic when asked to approve building datacenters down under.

Some sections of Australia’s population won’t mind it if big tech doesn’t show up: Protests against datacenters are already widespread.

Your correspondent recently spoke to the organizer of a protest group opposed to development of a new datacenter which is just three kilometers from four existing bit barns, one of which abuts a sizable apartment complex and has operated without incident or opposition for years. The organizer was blissfully ignorant of those facilities and eventually said their group is opposed to AI in all forms. ®

#10091. PRX Part 4: Our Data Strategy

Welcome back! This is Part 4 of the PRX series. Parts 1 to 3 covered model architectures, training design, and a 24-hour speedrun. This time we're pulling back the curtain on the part that quietly underpins all of it: the data. Of all the things that shaped PRX's quality, the data pipeline was one of the least glamorous parts to build but nevertheless an important piece to get right. Here's what we did, what we'd do differently, and a few things we only learned the slow way.

In one sentence: we assemble training data from a mix of public and internal datasets, re-caption the images with a VLM, and turn the result into the streamable corpus we trained PRX on.

At a high level, the data pipeline looks like this:

In the following we will dive into it in detail.

The goal was to assemble a large, diverse dataset for pre-training. At this stage the model is learning how the world looks: the visual concepts, the objects and scenes, how things are composed and lit, and the sheer range of what images can contain. That is a problem of coverage and diversity, not of per-image perfection. A broad, representative corpus teaches the model far more about the structure of the visual world than a smaller, prettier one would, even if many of the individual images are ordinary snapshots or slightly compressed. Over-filtering for aesthetics at this stage would actually hurt, narrowing the distribution and costing the model concepts and compositional variety it cannot recover later. Making generations look polished is a separate, later concern, which we leave to fine-tuning and preference alignment on small, ruthlessly curated sets. Pre-training is for breadth; fine-tuning is for taste.

We assemble our pre-training data from a mix of public and internal datasets. The priority at this stage is breadth, diversity, and standing on curation that already exists rather than redoing it ourselves. Where a source already comes quality-filtered, deduplicated, and filtered for NSFW content and personal information, we build on that work instead of repeating it at scale. Sources arrive in different shapes: some come with the image data itself, others as metadata plus baseline captions that we bring into a common form. We took a pragmatic approach: rather than build a corpus entirely from scratch, we leaned on existing datasets and our own tooling to assemble one quickly. In hindsight it is not necessarily the absolute best dataset one could build, but it was a solid and lightweight starting point for pre-training a 7B model.

In our experience, what matters most for pre-training is to use long captions that accurately describe everything in the image. We saw this directly in Part 2, where switching from short captions to long ones substantially improved sample quality. If captioning is faithful, we don't need to worry about the occasional screenshot, advertisement, logo, or bit of text in an image, because those things get described in the caption too, so the model learns them as conditioned, controllable attributes rather than reproducing them unconditionally. Accurate captioning turns "noise" into something you can prompt for, or prompt away. This is precisely why the filtering we do later is deliberately light. We remove what is genuinely unusable, not everything that is imperfect.

We have been using Mosaic Streaming and Mosaic Data Shards (MDS) as a dataset format for distributed training for a while now. In combination with Mosaic Composer we found it to be a very low-maintenance, flexible, and well-performing framework for distributed training. Furthermore, MDS datasets can easily and effectively be mixed and shuffled and also allow for distributed training directly from object storage like S3 or GCS.

However, MDS datasets are very rigid. Adding a column or creating a subset for a given filter basically means that one has to scan and rewrite the whole dataset. That's why we use Lance for this kind of feature engineering and dataset curation. Lance is a columnar data format with cheap predicate pushdown, scalar indexes, and vector search, the right tool for building and exploring datasets with billions of rows.

These two formats play off each other throughout this post and the PRX data pipeline: Lance to build, MDS to stream.

For previous training runs, we used T5Gemma as the text encoder and pre-computed the text latents, storing them in MDS as bytes. This time around, after switching the text encoder to Qwen3-VL, we decided to compute text latents on the fly during training instead. Running the text encoder inside the training loop costs throughput, but how much depends on the model: for a small denoiser it can be significant, whereas at PRX's 7B scale the text encoder's compute is negligible next to the denoiser, and we measured only a roughly 3–4% throughput cost (about 1 extra day on a 30-day run). In return we get two things. Skipping pre-computation keeps our MDS shards much smaller, small enough to store the full pre-training dataset on the SSD-backed shared filesystem of our SLURM cluster rather than streaming it over the network from object storage. And it keeps us free to change the text encoder later without rewriting terabytes of stored latents, which is exactly the kind of switch we made when moving to Qwen3-VL.

We encoded all images as JPEG at quality 92, instead of a lossless format such as PNG. We did not just assume quality 92 was safe, we measured it. Real-world images have usually already been JPEG-compressed several times, so the real question is whether one more re-encode hurts. Across repeated decode/encode cycles on both high-resolution (1–2 MP) and lower-resolution (0.25–0.5 MP) real images, the first re-encode at quality 92 is essentially imperceptible. Each further cycle adds almost nothing, because JPEG quickly converges to a stable state, and even after 10 cycles the images stay well within the imperceptible range, while PNG would be 3–10× larger for no perceptual gain. The numbers, averaged over 100 images at quality 92 and measured against the original (higher PSNR and lower LPIPS are better):

Since most source images already arrive JPEG-compressed, storing them losslessly as PNG buys little, so we convert everything to JPEG at high quality (quality 92).

We also checked what matters most: whether training on JPEGs changes what the model produces. Our corpus is mostly JPEG anyway, so the only advantage PNG could offer is not introducing new artifacts. We deliberately drew the comparison from high-resolution sources, on the expectation that even originally-JPEG images carry few artifacts at high resolution. We trained two identical PRX models at 1024px on the same images, one stored as PNG and one as JPEG at quality 92. Both trained equally well on our metrics, and their generations were practically indistinguishable, including when we estimated how JPEG-compressed the outputs look using a known technique for estimating JPEG quality by matching quantization tables:

The detection rate is the fraction of generations in which any quantization structure is found at all. The mean and median estimated JPEG quality are taken over only those flagged images. The two models are practically indistinguishable: only about one generation in ten from either shows any detectable quantization structure, and the differences are small enough that we are confident the training image format has a minimal effect on output quality. So high-quality JPEG storage adds nothing measurable on top of what the sources already carry. For large-scale text-to-image training that is more than good enough. For artifact-sensitive data used to train other Photoroom models, such as our custom AI Shadows model, we still rely on PNGs.

You cannot interactively explore Parquet tables with hundreds of millions or even billions of rows. We therefore store the data in Lance, where we can index, query, and browse it. We run the ingest with Ray Data, reading the source tables in parallel and writing many fragments of a Lance table across the cluster.

One lesson worth sharing is about fragmentation. A Lance table is split into fragments, and several operations scale with the total number of fragments rather than the row count: a scan opens the files of every fragment, and some metadata operations are O(number of fragments). A table broken into too many small fragments therefore queries slowly no matter its size. The Lance performance guidance is to keep that count low (the rule of thumb is on the order of a hundred fragments even for a billion-row table) and to run compaction periodically to merge small fragments into larger ones.

We learned this the slow way. Our first ingest targeted only 100,000 rows per fragment, which left thousands of tiny fragments and made even simple filters and full-text queries crawl. After compacting up to roughly a million rows per fragment, which for our tables of several hundred million rows meant on the order of a thousand fragments, queries were fast and we stopped worrying about it. The right target depends on row width, query patterns, and how the data is written, and in hindsight fewer, larger fragments might have been a better default. Lance supports distributed compaction (for example via the Lance-Ray integration), so it is easy to adjust after the fact, but it pays not to over-fragment in the first place.

We chose to re-caption every image ourselves rather than rely on the captions some of the datasets happened to ship with. The reason is consistency: across a mix of sources, caption length, style, and quality vary a lot, and we wanted a single uniform standard across the whole corpus (more on the captioner in Section 3).

The metadata a dataset already carries is still valuable, though, just for a different purpose. Pre-existing captions, and the vector embeddings that sometimes come alongside them (for example CLIP embeddings), are what make a dataset explorable in Lance right away: full-text search over the captions and nearest-neighbor search over an embedding column let us navigate the data and quickly judge its quality and the filtering it will need, well before we have run our own captioning over it. So we keep both, joining them in when they live in a separate table, and lean on them for the browsing we describe next.

With the data queryable, we could quickly profile it. The resolution distribution, for example, told us where to set cutoffs. Our smallest training bucket is 512² pixels, and we cap upscaling into a bucket at 4/3 (about 33%), so the effective cutoff is 384² ≈ 147k pixels plus an aspect ratio in [0.5, 2.0]. Everything below that we discard.

Lance tables support full-text search on text columns as well as nearest-neighbor similarity search on vector embedding columns out of the box, and both can be accelerated by building indexes. We did exactly that for the caption and embedding columns, then built a small UI to browse the dataset: real-time text search over the captions as well as navigating clusters of visually similar images via vector search.

Browsing the data this way let us assess its diversity and quality qualitatively and spot issues early, simply by looking at it. We found uninformative baseline captions, a surprising amount of non-photographic content (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics), and some near-duplicate images. These observations shaped the rest of the pipeline directly: re-caption everything (longer, accurate captions describe even imperfect images well, and guarantee that the caption matches the exact image we train on), and add light filtering and deduplication passes later. In general, we believe this sort of exploration tool is invaluable for getting a feel for a dataset before committing to it.

We found that long, detailed captions are a very strong lever on output quality. In an early benchmark we trained a small diffusion model twice on the same images, once on captions we generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and once on much shorter captions (produced with LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B), and scored both over training. The long captions generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B won across the board, with lower FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD at every checkpoint (lower is better on all three).

A small diffusion model trained on Qwen2.5-VL-7B captions (red) versus the baseline LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B captions (blue), scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three metrics.

Here is an example image with both our long, VLM-generated caption as well as the shorter caption used as the baseline:

Our captioning runs as a streaming pipeline built on Ray Data: it reads the data from Lance, prepares each image, captions it on the GPU, and writes the caption back as a new column we can query and filter on. We prompt for a single dense, visually grounded paragraph rather than a one-line caption.

A tight schedule and limited resources meant that we couldn't spend too much time on ablations of different captioning models and system prompts.

We used the following prompts to generate the captions.

We shortlisted three VLMs as captioner candidates:

We benchmarked caption quality indirectly: we trained a small diffusion model for 100k steps on each caption variant and scored its generations with FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD. Alongside the three candidates we scored two reference captioners, to connect this comparison to the first benchmark: the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B (the same model as in the benchmark above) and a set of Gemini 1.5 Flash captions we had generated earlier for the 1M-image internal test set used here. The Gemini captions are a similar length but were produced with a different prompt (all others use the system prompt above), so its curve is indicative rather than a like-for-like comparison.

FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD over training for the three captioner candidates and two reference captioners, scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three.

Among the candidates, Qwen3.5-9B is best on all three metrics, with Qwen3-VL-8B close behind on FID and DINO-MMD (though weaker on CMMD) and the Relaxed captioner trailing on FID but competitive elsewhere. The clearest result is that the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B — the same model that beat the baseline in the first benchmark — is now the weakest of the five, which is exactly why we didn't just keep it: a caption-tuned or newer model measurably helps. (Gemini 1.5 Flash lands mid-pack, but with the different-prompt caveat above.)

We put less weight on throughput than quality, but at hundreds of millions of images it still matters, since it sets how much the captions cost to generate. We measured it only for the three candidates, all served through vLLM with no quantization or custom kernels. The tuning was at the pipeline level: one vLLM replica per GPU, with enough Ray Data pool workers to keep all eight GPUs on a node saturated. We first found Qwen3-VL-8B to be the fastest (20 img/s per H200) and chose it, for its speed, quality, and stable, release-grade vLLM support. Only later did we find that the Qwen2.5-VL "Relaxed" captioner reaches the same 20 img/s once fixed: it had been saved with the wrong architecture class, which broke vLLM's torch.compile hashing and forced slow eager mode until we re-saved it as Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration. Qwen3.5-9B produces great captions but ran slower (~6.5 img/s) and needed unstable nightly dependency builds at the time. A few months on, it is probably a great choice too.

At the end of the pipeline, we turn the captioned, bucketed stream into MDS, the format the trainer streams.

The Mosaic Streaming library packs samples into ~128MB shards streamed during training from object storage or a local filesystem. Lance does support simple distributed training as well, but we found that converting to MDS is the lower friction path for us. Mosaic Streaming gives us, for free, the distributed-training machinery we'd otherwise have to build ourselves:

Diffusion training runs on fixed-size tensors, so every image in a batch must share one width and height. Rather than crop everything square (losing the sides of portraits and landscapes) or pad (wasting compute), we use aspect-ratio bucketing: a small set of allowed (w, h) shapes, with each image snapped to the nearest one and only same-shape images batched together.

We bucket in two steps. First by resolution tier (pixel count): a 512px and a 1024px tier for most of the corpus, plus 2048px and 4096px tiers for high-resolution data. An image goes into the largest tier it can reach without upscaling by more than 4/3 (~33%), so each tier's floor is (size × 3/4)² (≈384² for the 512 tier, 768² for 1024); anything below the smallest floor is dropped. Then by aspect ratio within the tier: we enumerate the patch-aligned (w, h) shapes (both divisible by 16, AR in [0.5, 2.0]) that keep a roughly constant ~256-patch token budget, giving 13 buckets per tier, from 0.5 (tall) through 1.0 (square) to 2.0 (wide). At 512px that's 352×704 … 512×512 … 704×352; at 1024px the same 13 ratios scaled up. Constant patch count keeps per-image compute flat across shapes.

Each image is then resized to its bucket with a Lanczos filter and encoded as JPEG at quality 92, and Mosaic Data Shards are written into a tree keyed by resolution and aspect ratio so the trainer can stream buckets separately:

The exploration in Section 2 relied on whatever captions a dataset shipped with. Once our own detailed captions were in place, the same full-text search became far more powerful, and a few passes over the captions turned up things the sparser original metadata had hidden: more text-heavy images (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics) than we had estimated, and some NSFW content that had slipped through.

To turn those approximate searches into a filter, we ran a quick classification pass with Qwen3-8B in text-only mode: it reads each caption (never the image) and labels the sample visual, text, or nsfw. The whole heuristic is essentially one question, "Would you look at this image, or read it?" Classifying from the caption rather than the pixels is cheap (around 200 captions/s per GPU) and reuses work we had already done. A pixel-level image classifier would likely be more accurate, but this was good enough to remove the obvious cases at moderate cost and without having to annotate data and train a custom classifier.

Rather than rewrite the whole corpus to drop these samples, we added a skip-list feature to the MDS data loader: a small sidecar file per shard lists the sample indices to skip, and the loader unions them and skips those samples at training time. Nothing is deleted or rewritten. This turned out to be a flexible mechanism well beyond this one filter. We can exclude any set of examples identified after the fact, whether a newly discovered quality issue, a blacklist, or, importantly, data from users who later opt out of having their content used for training, simply by extending the skip list before the next run. It is also convenient for ablations: to measure a filter's effect, train once with the skip list and once without, off the same dataset, instead of storing two copies. The one limit is scale. Skip lists add a little per-sample work at load time, so once the skipped fraction grows large (we would estimate somewhere around 10%, though we have not measured the crossover), it becomes worth rewriting the MDS dataset without the skipped samples rather than carrying an ever-growing skip list.

The same explorer surfaced a fair number of duplicates: large image collections tend to accumulate exact and near-duplicate copies, which waste training compute and skew the distribution. We mainly targeted near-duplicates and exact copies, so we added a quick deduplication pass using perceptual hashes. If the goal is to identify duplicate concepts and balance them in a dataset, deduplication based on clusters of image embeddings is a more suitable approach.

We could have done an exact dedup on a byte hash like SHA-256, but a perceptual hash already subsumes that (it matches byte-identical images too) while also catching re-encoded or resized copies, so we used only the perceptual hash. It is a standard DCT-based perceptual hash (downscale to a small grayscale thumbnail, 2D DCT, threshold the low-frequency coefficients into a compact fingerprint), implemented in a few lines on top of OpenCV and SciPy. We consider two hashes a match if their Hamming distance is zero, so we only remove near-pixel-identical copies. Genuinely different shots of the same subject have different fingerprints (and different captions) and are kept on purpose.

Once every image has a perceptual hash (fingerprint), the dedup itself is just a hash-map lookup: scanning each aspect-ratio bucket across resolutions, we keep one entry per fingerprint, so any image whose fingerprint we have already seen is a duplicate of the one we kept, and when a cluster spans resolutions we keep the highest-resolution copy. The duplicates are written out as a per-shard skip list that the loader unions and skips at load time, so nothing is deleted and the dataset is never rewritten.

Across the corpus, deduplication removed on the order of a few percent of images, the caption-based text filter a few percent more, and the NSFW pass a small fraction of a percent.

The dataset described here is the pre-training corpus, where breadth and scale matter most. For supervised fine-tuning and preference alignment the trade flips entirely: quality matters far more than quantity, and the problem becomes finding and curating small, high-signal subsets out of this large corpus. To do that we have been building more powerful curation tooling, including a richer explorer that tags images with structured attributes predicted by a VLM so we can assemble highly targeted subsets for fine-tuning. We plan to dig into topics like fine-tuning and preference alignment as well as the data tooling we use for these in a future post.

Build something with PRX, or find a bug in our pipeline? PRX is Apache 2.0 and the model code lives at github.com/Photoroom/PRX. We integrated PRX into the diffusers library and there is a Hugging Face Space to try out our latest version PRX Pixel.

Come talk diffusion models and data with us on Discord.

Thanks so much, Photoroom team, for sharing your experiences from PRX so far!! Learned a lot.

GitHub now highlights ACCESSIBILITY.md files and helps maintainers document accessibility goals, known barriers, supported environments, contributor expectations, and reporting processes.

Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change.

An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers.

GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document.

GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works:

Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance.

New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work.

GitHub CLI’s accessibility statement, for example, documents settings, known barriers, and workarounds. It explains why table output can be difficult to follow with a screen reader and provides a command that prints pull request numbers and titles one per line instead. It also asks contributors changing prompts or output to show the results with relevant accessibility settings enabled. Developers using the CLI get a specific workaround; developers contributing to it get clear expectations for their changes.

The GitHub Annotation Toolkit’s accessibility statement documents a limitation of its Figma library: annotations use canvas position, connecting lines, and matching numbers to visually convey relationships. Access to individual canvas objects does not necessarily communicate what those relationships are.

The statement gives collaborators a concrete alternative: provide a structured text description that identifies each annotated element, its intended semantics and behavior, and any relevant ordering. For developers preparing or receiving a design handoff, this explains what information needs to accompany the visual annotations.

The file also explains how to report accessibility barriers and explicitly states that the library has not undergone keyboard-only or screen-reader testing. Readers get both practical guidance and clear limits on what the project has verified. Showing this information in the repository overview makes it easier to find alongside the project’s other documentation.

There is no one fixed format for an ACCESSIBILITY.md file. A small library, command-line tool, documentation site, and large web application have different users, risks, and maintenance capacity. Start with accurate information that the project can keep current.

Keep in mind that a project can name a Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version and level as a target. A target does not establish verified conformance. A conformance claim requires an evaluation and should identify the evaluated scope, date, method, and evaluator.

The most useful accessibility statements serve people who arrive after something has already gone wrong. Plain language, descriptive links, and a clear reporting route matter more than legal or standards-heavy language.

Useful reporting guidance invites relevant context, such as the affected task, page, observed behavior, browser, operating system, and assistive technology. It makes screenshots and recordings optional and avoids asking someone to prove a disability.

The statement should also set expectations that maintainers can consistently meet. That can include acknowledgement, status updates, available workarounds, expected timelines, and an opportunity for the reporter to verify a fix.

The Open Source Accessibility Toolkit provides a detailed public example.

GitHub’s Community Standards workflow provides a shorter starter with prompts that projects can replace with their own information. The goal is not to produce a perfect policy before publishing the file. Start with accurate information, name the gaps, and update the statement as the project’s accessibility practices mature.

Adding an accessibility statement makes accessibility work more discoverable to users, contributors, and maintainers. Normalizing that practice across open source projects helps make accessibility part of how communities plan, build, report, and improve their work.

Add an accessibility statement to your repository >

Jan Maarten (he/him) is a designer and accessibility specialist living on unceded Duwamish lands. He brings two decades of experience across product design, brand, strategy, and leadership. At GitHub, he bridges design and engineering to improve accessible products, evolve design-system infrastructure, and create resources for the wider design community, including the open-source GitHub Annotation Toolkit.

#10089. OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models

How much damage can a rogue agent do in 35 seconds? Asking cos that’s how long it might take to shut one down

In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior.

“As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post.

The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.”

The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster.

“The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises.

A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.”

OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one.

The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development.

“Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.”

OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.”

That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

GitHub’s new Git storage architecture is built so thousands of agents can push to a single repository at once. Here’s how it works.

Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.

Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post, we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.

We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.

The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.

We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:

Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.

We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.

We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:

On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.

In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.

Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.

Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

Spokes routes a repository’s traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository’s other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.

When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository’s packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.

Let’s walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:

There are many distinct approaches we’ve taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let’s dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.

Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:

Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.

References are the opposite. A busy repository’s references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.

Our first approach was a write-ahead log for all of a repository’s references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It’s correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn’t, it’s done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository’s write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.

Our second approach split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it’s only as fast as the slowest segment. We’d traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:

Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the last post was still somewhere in the stack. Here’s how it works.

Each reference update in Ref-CAS is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum. A transaction locks only the references it touches, checks that each one still has the value the writer expects, and becomes visible once a majority of the log’s replicas have recorded it. Agents mostly push to their own branches, so most updates don’t contend, and they replicate in parallel. When two pushes do update the same reference, only one will append to the log.

Each commit to Ref-CAS gets a log sequence number (LSN), and the repository’s version is the LSN of its latest commit. Reads start with a version check against that version. A virtual replica sends the version of the reference state it already holds. If that version is still current, the reply carries no references at all, and an unchanged repository costs a single comparison. If the virtual replica is behind, it gets back the current references and version, along with pointers to pack data and anything else that needs to be known, such as when the last garbage collection cycle occurred.

Unlike the consensus group in our legacy architecture, Ref-CAS never holds or validates object data. It only stores pointers to it. A virtual replica uploads a push’s pack to Blob Storage before it commits the reference transaction. A reference only ever points at objects that are already durable.

These approaches allow us to transact reference state alone in the tens of thousands of operations per second, and provide a baseline for additional annotations on the replication log that help reads decide what to download for a given request.

But supporting thousands of writes per second on a single repository creates a second-order problem: maintaining the performance of reads and writes. For that, we needed a different approach to compaction.

Every push adds a pack to Blob Storage. Git can serve a repository from many packs, but each additional pack makes lookups slightly more expensive, so the pack count can’t grow without bound. In our legacy architecture, compaction runs on the same replicas that serve traffic, and it has to run on every replica. In the new architecture, it runs entirely in the background on separate nodes, directly against durable storage, using the Ref-CAS service to notify virtual replicas of the evolving state.

Compaction nodes each claim ownership over a subset of the repository’s data via a lease, which allows us to scale compaction horizontally. Here’s how one compaction node works through a single shard of a repository’s packs:

The node first takes a lease on the shard in Blob Storage, so only one node compacts a shard at a time. Meanwhile, virtual replicas keep uploading packs and listing them in the pack manifest. The node reads the manifest to find new packs and collects them into an open segment, which is effectively a holding ground for data about to be compacted. When the segment reaches a defined limit based on pack count, size, or age, it seals the segment so it accepts no new packs, then combines its packs into fewer, larger ones. While compaction happens, the next segment for the shard can begin capturing its input packs. Before anything is published, the node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects as the inputs. It then uploads the new packs and adds them to the manifest. A second transaction removes the inputs from the manifest, and cleanup deletes them later.

To scale out, this process runs independently for many shards at once. Each pack’s hash maps to a shard, so adding shards and nodes adds compaction throughput. A compacted pack that’s still under the size limit goes back into a shard by its own hash and merges again, so packs grow in tiers until they reach the limit. The net result is an effectively flat pack count while pushes climb:

Compaction merges packs, but it keeps every object. Garbage collection is the step that removes objects nothing references anymore, like the ones left behind by deleted branches and force-pushes. In our new architecture, garbage collection works very similarly to compaction by using dedicated workers to handle the compute-heavy portion. It also has a few special behaviors for safely removing data, which are worthy of their own discussion.

Using these approaches, we’ve been able to consistently demonstrate a flat latency curve as writes climb, and we have other planned optimizations to make the compaction and garbage collection processes themselves more performant.

The two principles we started with let each part of this architecture scale on its own. We scale reads and writes by adding virtual replicas. Ref-CAS orders each reference independently instead of the whole repository. We scale maintenance by adding compaction nodes. Our goal is for every repository, from one developer’s side project to the busiest monorepo, to run on the same architecture with no special handling for the busy ones. Repositories don’t stay small. A side project can pick up a fleet of agents overnight, and it shouldn’t need a migration or special handling from us to keep up. One architecture also means every improvement we make reaches every repository at once.

This foundation lets us do a lot more. We’re focused on three areas next: scaling the architecture beyond what we can predict we’ll need today, making agents more efficient at the work they do on GitHub, and evolving Git itself for agentic development.

We have plans to take this architecture further. Each of these improvements lets a repository handle more activity while reducing the work behind each request:

Scaling the infrastructure is one side of supporting agents. The other side is making each agent operation cheaper: fewer bytes to fetch, fewer round trips, and less waiting on changes. Each of these fast-follow items builds on the storage work in this post:

We also have work to do in Git itself. GitHub has been a longtime contributor to the Git project, and we’re not stopping now. A few examples of the work we’re excited to continue:

Agents have changed how software gets built. GitHub and Git are changing with it. We’re excited to take this new architecture across the starting line. It’s available in a limited private preview now, with a broader rollout early next year. We can’t wait to see what teams build when the number of agents working on a repository is limited by their ideas. We’ll keep evolving Git and GitHub alongside our customers and the Git community.

Brian is a Principal Software Engineer working on the storage and core services that power all repository interactions on GitHub.
