When I was working for a startup in the early 2000s, we had our own servers. We were growing, so were adding servers at a pretty good clip. After one particular expansion, all of a sudden, Saturday night at 3 am, we blew breaker. No one had a good explanation, but the sysadmins were not happy about needing to go to the office in the middle of the night to fix things up.

A week later, the same thing happened. I suggested that it was the RAID check kickoff that might be doing it. And, indeed, it was. A couple of dozen servers all seeking their drives at once was too much for the circuits they were on. Staggering the startup time fixed it.

Coherence can be good, like when you're rowing crew, or bad, like when you have dozens of drives all drawing max power. Or, from the summary, gazoober UPS systems doing a battery check.

Having corporate IT experience from administration to manufacture of banking systems, the system is supposed to be on a breaker that covers its maximum possible load, and such load be used in the calculations for sharing breakers. Wherever you worked was doing it wrong. The added amps from drive actuation should have been in the total breaker calculation along with maximum memory and CPU usage.

Simply staggering the array check time to slip by meant your circuit breakers were already on-edge without a safe margin, but my money is on your employer never fixing the problem after it was found.

Maximum amperage draw for 1/10th of a second is not usually taken into account, breakers don't usually blow that fast because of a current spike. (Those numbers are usually not on the specification sheet either.)

The maximum load is calculated over a period of time, not a very short period of time. It is in this fuzzy gap that issues like this arrive.

Maximum amperage draw for 1/10th of a second is not usually taken into account, breakers don't usually blow that fast because of a current spike. (Those numbers are usually not on the specification sheet either.)

Breakers are analog devices. They have a trip curve which specifies the amount of current it will take to trip them. This is to handle inrush current as well as perform their duty to protect the wiring behind the walls.

The trip curve is time to trip versus current. And it can be surprisingly long -

Motor starting inrush current is massive compared to the running current, but it happens so briefly that it *usually* doesn't matter. An AC unit that runs at 8-9 amperes may take 90-100 amps or more to start, causing blown breakers, or even main breakers if the system is being taxed by another high current job like running an oven or charging a car. Nobody runs a 100 amp circuit to an AC system that calls for a 15 amp circuit, and neither does the unit have lugs big enough to accommodate that kind of wiring

#10049. Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit

Outage hits login, software repositories, and patching tools hours before online event kicks off

A swathe of Canonical's web services has been offline for hours, an awkward warm-up for tomorrow's Ubuntu Summit.

Canonical's status page lists widespread disruption beginning at approximately 1100 UTC, affecting gopkg.in, Ubuntu cloud images and mailing lists, jaas.ai, the Ubuntu keyserver, Launchpad PPAs, the Livepatch API, canonical.com, Ubuntu login, maas.io, and 16 other services. Landscape is also affected. Email and the company's Discourse forums remain available.

The Register has asked Canonical for more information but had received no response at publication time. The company suffered a DDoS attack last month, although the cause of this outage has not been confirmed.

The timing is unfortunate. As the banner across the top of the Discourse forum page says: "The Ubuntu Summit starts tomorrow – join from anywhere!"

The online event runs on November 12-13. For the first time since the 2022 Summit in Prague, The Reg FOSS desk won't be attending in person.

Canonical is still experimenting with the format of the event, and the last few have been primarily online, with just a small in-person audience in its London offices. This is the second of two Summits this year, labeled 26.04 and 26.10 to mirror Ubuntu's release cycle.

The timetable, hosted on the Discourse site, lists several talks on AI and agentic coding. The AI-heavy program we reported from June's event appears to be continuing. ®

#10048. Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card

Iâve discovered a voltage fault injection vulnerability on the GA100 die, allowing an operator to blow arbitrary fuses. Utilizing this vulnerability, Iâve converted my CMP 170HX 8GB card into what is effectively an A100-80G! Further, my unlocked cards actually perform ~1.2x faster than a retail A100 by having all functional SMs enabled (~120-126, die-lottery dependent), rather than the yield-safe 108 SMs NVIDIA chose for all production A100 cards. Finally, CMP-disabled features like NVLink, PCIe Gen4, NVJPG, NVDEC, MIG are all unlockable with this approach, though I havenât specifically tested NVJPG/NVDEC/MIG.

Hereâs how my âA100-80Gâ appears and functions.

NVIDIA uses fuses for product segmentation, security features, and other fun access control features - and crucially, there are several functions where blowing a fuse on an NVIDIA die can grant you more access, not less. In a properly secured design, a blown fuse should always induce a more restrictive state, because a blown fuse cannot be unblown in an economically feasible way. NVIDIAâs design allows one to relax restrictions by blowing more fuses!

In this post, I will go over the GA100 die, its fuse controller, the use of VFI, and future research directions. Iâve decided to publish some of the work that enabled my research here.

My work builds on prior research by Jon Pry and numerous others who have dedicated much of their time towards better understanding the GA100 die. I am disclosing my findings subsequent to another security researcher independently discovering the same vulnerability; I believe it to be in the best interest of the public to make this information publicly available. These findings were disclosed to NVIDIAâs product security team ahead of the publication of this article.

The GA100 is an NVIDIA die that has been used to power almost 20 different SKUs - the A100 being the most well-known variant. I wonât delve into every SKU, but I will present the GA100 manifestations that matter to my work, covering the different versions of the CMP 170HX and the A100.

As fabbed, the GA100 die has 128 SMs, 12 FBPs, 5 NVDEC units, a PCIe Gen4 x16 controller, and depending on the framebuffer size, comes with 4-6 stacks of HBM co-packaged with the die. NVIDIA uses eFuses for yield-control and product segmentationâundifferentiated GA100s turn into more restrictive variants based on defect testing and manufacturer demand.

In one of the most extreme manifestations of product segmentation, the CMP 170HX, an Ethereum mining card with nominally 8 or 10 GB of application-exposed framebuffer capacity, actually comes with, respectively, ~80 and ~40 GB of HBM onboard! This work chiefly centers around how to fully unlock and use that capacity. Previous work has made great strides in unlocking the GA100 via software methods; VFI takes us across the last mile.

So, how does NVIDIA utilize fuses to produce both a datacenter A100 and a mining CMP card from one die? To understand this, we need to take a closer look at the fuse controller located on the GA100.

The fuse controller is a block that contains 16,384 eFuses (512 rows of 32) and a bunch of logic surrounding that raw fuse macro. Its job is to perform fuse readout and programming, protect the underlying fuses, and provide usable âoption wordsâ to the rest of the die. These option words subsequently decide how the die functions and what features are enabled.

Each eFuse can be in one of two states (blown=1, unblown=0), and the 512 rows are divided into 4 regions:

There are two really interesting groups of fuses for the VFI-based unlock:

Before we name some of the FF-encoded option words, weâll have to first understand the FF record format in a bit more detail, then talk about the die blocks that govern the features we are interested in.

Each FF row is a 32-bit record. Bits 0â4 select a chain, bit 5 distinguishes FF from IFF (0 for FF), bits 6â15 select a 16-bit block, and bits 16â31 supply that blockâs new value. The JTAG-chain picture from the patent is quite literal here: the controller builds the option data by replaying these records into chains. Fixed locations in each chain correspond to individual option words.

If two records address the same chain and block, the later record wins. For example, 0x0fe805c1 means chain 1, block 23, data 0x0fe8. Appending that record can clear an effective bit set by an earlier FF record. No physical fuse is unblown; a new row replaces the old 16-bit block. This works for FF-backed options, not the regular control fuses in rows 0 and 1.

Now that we know how FF words are encoded, hereâs a list of the interesting words and their locations. These were discovered by a particularly helpful researcher who cross-compared FF values and effective option words from different GA100 SKUs in order to differentially understand the FF chain/block to option word mappings, as there is no known official mapping.

The acronyms FBIO/FBPA/FBP/TPC/GPC/PES/ROP all refer to microarchitectural elements, please see this diagram from the GA100 whitepaper to further understand how these are related to each other:

FBP is the internal NVIDIA term for a âframebuffer partitionâ, with 2 FBPs to one HBM stack. FBPAs are subpartitions, 2 FBPAs to one FBP. PES/ROP are blocks (seemingly graphics-related) that are required for an SM to function.

With this knowledge in hand, what if we could write new FF rows that set the _DISABLE words to be all zeroes, or at least, as permissive as possible given die defects? If we look at how the _DISABLE options are used in conjunction with other elements, weâll quickly see that these _DISABLE words are the primary lever we have in preventing parts of the die from being âfloorsweptâ. After illuminating the âwhat-ifâ, Iâll talk about the âhowâ: the exact application of voltage fault injection and the fuse controller safeguards we can defeat with VFI.

NVIDIA puts these options in charge of setting floorsweep signals, which will render a die element unreachable (and likely powered down). From experiments, I believe the floorsweep lines are specified in RTL, emanating from the fuse controller and terminating in individual functional blocks and controlling some master power/clock domain switch within the block. I have observed the floorsweeping behavior to correspond with very little latency with the value of the fuse controllerâs effective status words for each functional block.

Letâs take FBP floorsweeping, for example. On one of my 8 GB cards, OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852: FBPs 1, 4, 6, and 11 were masked. The separate OPT_FBP_DEFECTIVE mask was 0x840, covering 6 and 11. After I reduced the FF-backed disable mask to 0x840 with a replacement FF row, the extra masks on 1 and 4 were gone, but the defective 6 and 11 stayed disabled. That leaves 10 of the dieâs 12 FBPs in the effective mask. Functionally, FBPs 1 and 4, which refused register reads and writes when OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852, became responsive after this fuse write.

Although the functional blocks can be âunfloorsweptâ with FF writes, this does not fully suffice to render the block fully available to an end application - the default framebuffer geometry configuration uses only a portion of each available HBM stack, for example.

To bypass that, we can utilize what is essentially a small modification to cmpunlockerâs method. The usual driver patch for the 8 -> 64 GB unlocks writes to a particular set of feature configuration words (FBPA_CFG, SM_SPEED_SELECT, etc.). The default values are chosen to succeed for the commonly found variant of the 170HX, which has the _DISABLE FF-derived option words preventing certain functional blocks from being used (any attempt to use them will return floorswept errors). With the unlocking FF burns in place, we can write even more permissive words into the configuration registers, resulting in what is functionally an A100-80G.

With the information we have, it seems straightforward that if one could blow arbitrary FF fuses, any GA100 could be fully unlocked to its maximum capability, as determined by die yield and the populated memory stacks. But how do we blow FF fuses? Letâs take a look at the fuse programming functionality of the fuse controller to understand more.

To request a fuse blow, one must write to the FUSEADDR, FUSEWDATA, and FUSECTRL registers belonging to the fuse controller. Although not nominally accessible to the host or to unprivileged requesters, with the Canary in the Crypto Mine ROP, opening up the responsible privilege level masks is trivial. And so, many researchers have attempted to coerce the fuse controller to blow fuses in the FF region. Some of our shared observations follow:

The specific option word I am referring to is OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE (âSBFEâ), and it is set to be 1 in all production cards. When this option word is clear, fuse programming is allowed in any address. When it is set, only FPF fuses may be blown. To date, no one has found any way to burn FF fuses with SBFE=1, even when operating the fuse controller from HS contexts. It is not clear what âsecured burnâ truly means, I speculate that there must be a software-only way to perform non-FPF burns even with SBFE=1, and we just donât know what the âsecuredâ adjective really means here.

Note PLM, HS, ucode, â¦; I am delving into using a bunch of NVIDIA-specific terminology in this section as the explanation gets deeper. For a really in-depth explanation of what these mean, I refer you to other sources such as Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon.

Importantly, as people have figured out on more permissive cards, it is possible to perform FF burns with SBFE=0! And as it turns out, achieving this state is how we achieve the GA100 unlock. After much trial-and-error, I have resorted to inducing this state via voltage fault injection, and I was able to achieve it. Letâs talk some more about voltage glitching.

Much has been said about VFI, and Iâll leave the in-depth explanation to other sources. In short, applying brief pulses of low supply voltage will often cause unexpected behavior in integrated circuits. I asked GPT-6 Astra to design an STM32G4 based board that taps into the PWMVID signal on the CMP PCB. PWMVID is an NVIDIA standard for voltage regulators, and my glitcher intercepts the PWM signal emitted by the GA100 die, and replaces it with its own waveform fed into the MP2888B VRM driver IC. With my setup, I can induce the cardâs own VRM to produce timed glitches for me, which is simpler than MOSFET-based setups and enables faster glitching than attempting to directly drive the PMBus.

The glitcher requires two connections to the PCB, ideally done with magnet/enameled wire. One wire taps NVVDD for voltage sensing, and another wire taps the PWMVID signal. The only other required step for the glitcher to function is the removal of a 0402 0ohm resistor, which will break the connection between the GA100 output PWM pin and the VRM IC. Finding where to place the taps is trivial by tracing the pinout of the MP2888B, specifically its PWMVID and VOSEN pins (the MP2888B shares a footprint with its sibling public chip MP2888A). Test points directly adjacent to the MP2888B enable relatively easy installation of the PWMVID tap.

With this tap in place, a single glitch attempt involves this sequence:

My setup achieves steps 1/2 with a simple ACPI S0 -> S3 -> S0 transition, which can be done in a few seconds on a modern desktop platform. More intrusive modifications or expensive rigs can probably achieve a better experiment rate, but in my experience this setup suffices to unlock cards in somewhere between 1 hour and 48 hours of glitching time using the approach described later.

For the NVVDD threshold, the Astra-authored firmware uses an STM32 comparator to detect when NVVDD crosses 225mV, after which a tight DMA loop drives the desired duties on the PWMVID pin. After S0, the host inspects the card state and decides what to do next; if it involves another glitch, the glitcher board will be commanded over USB with a glitch pattern. Then the host induces S3 with an RTC timer to wake back up in ~3s (empirically derived period for decent stability).

Sometimes the host will fail to return to S0, Iâve remedied this with relegating bookkeeping and glitch campaign preparation to an SBC (Radxa Cubie A5E) which also can drive the motherboard power/reset button pins via GPIO if the glitch target host is unresponsive.

More specifics are shared in the GA100VFI repository if youâre interested. For now, letâs take a look at the different interesting states we can trigger via VFI, as well as the specific glitch state that we need to burn FF rows. To help illuminate the differences between each glitch state, I have built an empirical model of how the fuse controller starts up when voltage is applied. Note that without the RTL that implements the fuse controller, all we have are guesses. Here are the hypothesized boot stages:

These hypothetical stages are based on what I can actually read from the die: controller states, raw rows when CMD_READ works, the published option words, and whether the PRI ring can still reach the rest of the GPU. By looking at a few key values, we can tell glitch outcomes apart. Importantly, glitch patterns and outcomes are very much die-specific, so consider these example waveforms and responses to be just that, examples. Letâs take a look at 3 interesting glitch states.

Some glitches make almost every published option word read as zero. In one captured state, 669 of 672 named option reads were zero; the other three were error responses. The controllerâs CRC status was 0x00 (not parsed yet), the PCIe ID read as 2080 (the base GA100 PCIe product ID, does not correspond to a real retail product), and the GPUâs PRI ring was held in reset.

This state is consistent with a catastrophic failure on behalf of the fuse controller. The card comes up basically unusable, because almost all boot functions are disrupted by the all-zero state. However, interesting enough, the card trains at PCIe Gen4 natively! Some slightly altered variants may showcase sections of fuses being successfully latched, or containing garbled values instead of all-zeroes. I was not able to push any of these states towards an FF burn; in almost all of them the fuse controller is unreachable or dysfunctional.

Reading the RIR data on the CMP 170HX 8GB reveals its exact effect: 15 noop repair instructions, and one write that changes the value of a fuse in row 18, whose option word we can monitor. Further, because the RIR sense is consumed internally by the fuse macro instead of directly by the fuse controller, we can observe a disrupted RIR latch by attempting to read the raw row - the observed bitflip remains consistent across the flipped option word as well as the raw fuse row. This sets an interesting chronological checkpoint in investigating die boot (RIR sense must happen prior to other fuse sensing), but is not a useful glitch in itself.

The successful three-pulse state on my first card seemed to disrupt precisely the row0/1 based option words, while leaving other fuses and option words intact. In this state, all of the row0/1 derived option words are zero. The initial readbacks look like this:

At this stage, we are still not yet capable of issuing FF writes, because ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0. I am honestly not sure why ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM would ever be zero, given itâs 1 in retail boards, so this almost reads to me like a way to implement a glitch-detection canary (or at least it would be elegant to do so).

Fuse sensing happens one row at a time, with all 32 fuses powered for sensing with one line, meaning it is much more challenging for an attacker to make a single fuse appear as cleared or set. It would make sense, then, to include a âcanaryâ fuse that disables security-critical features (like fuse burning) when it is cleared, because usually the attacker can only manipulate fuse sensing at the row granularity at most. So, when the row0/1 option words come up as all cleared, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0 stops us from burning any fuses.

However, take a look at what we have in this state: DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE=0. This word is normally 1, and it stops us from setting the EN_SW_OVERRIDE register to 1, which then lets us âshadowâ most of the option words exposed by the fuse controller. Doing so involves writing to a register CTRL_OPT_*, corresponding to option word OPT_*, which then determines the effective value STATUS_OPT_*. This is what lets us shadow SBFE to be 0. But, even though we have DSOV=0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM turns out to be one of the option words that are impossible to shadow, even with DSOV=0. So it seems weâre stuck.

At least thatâs what I thought, and I banged my head against the wall in this state for a while. Then I noticed that there is one fuse controller command I havenât tried issuing yet: SENSE_CTRL. I had refrained from issuing this, because on the face of it it seems like all of the row0/1 (control fuse) derived option words would match their fused values, which would reset SBFE, turn off software option word shadowing, and leave us unable to fuse. To my surprise, when I issued this command, all of the control-fuse-derived options went to their fused value, except DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE, which remained 0!

With DSOV=0, we can trivially set SBFE to 0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM is 1 because it matches its fused value, and we are off to the races! One wrinkle remains in that FUSEWDATA may have a locked down PLM, but with DSOV=0, we can just write 0 to OPT_SECURE_FUSE_WDATA_WR_SECURE to set the PLM to be all-ones, opening host access for fusing.

At this point, all thatâs left to do is to calculate _DISABLE words that match the _DEFECTIVE values for the features we are interested in, and issue FF burns. Note that the occupied FF space and defective bits differ per die, so each burn must be die-tailored.

On 8 GB cards with 80 GB intact (seems to be around ~90% of 8 GB cards from my limited sample size), the unlock yields the full 80 GB as a usable framebuffer. Multiple synthetic tests (writing pseudorandom words throughout the full framebuffer and reading them back after L2 invalidation) as well as real workloads (such as vLLM and SGLand) are fully functional. As mentioned, one of my cards has only 64 GB intact. In this case, the hardware unlock yields no framebuffer advantage.

The 170HX is limited to 70 SMs out of the box. In practice, there are almost always >120 SMs non-defective on the die, and the unlock allows using them all. This results in a significant performance uplift, ~1.7x compared to the software-only 170HX unlock, and even an impressive ~1.2x over a retail A100!

The only thing that stops cmpunlocker from advancing beyond PCIe Gen2 are the FF option words. With relevant bits cleared, Gen3/4 train and are confirmed to be fully functional. When combined with the PCIe decoupling capacitor mod, up to PCIe Gen4 x16 is attainable, matching a retail A100 PCIe variant.

Zeroing out the OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE word is only one of the required mods for NVLink to actually work. Because the CMP 170HX PCB is missing the U11 IC (which connects PCIe 3.3v to an NVLink bridge pin), a stock board fails to bring up the reference clock generator on attached NVLink bridges. Simply bridging two of the pins on the footprint of U11 resolves this issue, although it removes whatever regulation or protection was provided by U11. Be careful if youâre bridging GPUs powered by different power supplies, as this will connect the +3.3V rails together unless you leave U11 unpopulated on some of your GPUs! The NVLink bridge works fine if you just patch U11 on one of the boards in the pair.

On the firmware side of NVLink enablement, there is a ROM check that needs to be bypassed with additional host-side commands. Iâm sure your clanker can figure it out ;)

While investigating the NVLink unlock, I also found a few interesting quirks with NVIDIAâs NVLink implementation on the GA100. I will be posting a further blog post on this, so stay tuned!

With arbitrary fuse burning, we mostly gain feature unlocks. Some security-sensitive options are shipped unblown by default, and burning them may lead to interesting footholds. But whatâs more interesting to me are the deeper glitch states where many default-blown security-sensitive fuses sense unblown, enabling routes like debug HS execution, which grant unprecedented access to die internals.

Anecdotally, out of the 10 specimens of CMP 170HX 8 GB I have examined, only one has shipped with only 64 GB usable, the rest all have a functional framebuffer size of 80 GB. â©

Although the Canary in the Crypto Mine paper claims a stable 80 GB on the 10 GB SKU, very few, if any, cards in the wild have been able to achieve this, and solid evidence is scarce. It remains plausible that some number of 10 GB SKUs really do come shipped with 80 GB on-board, however the percentage seems very low according to the community. Most âunstableâ 80 GB unlocks are explained with a combination of L2 caching and memory aliasing over a true 40 GB framebuffer. â©

Enabling NVLink further requires a very small hardware mod due to a missing component on the 170HX PCB, Iâll talk more about this later. â©

#10047. NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

Surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

World foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

The key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

The bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

The teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are important: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

To improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

The teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

Autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

Cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

The resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

While Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a new frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

The immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a new family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

Real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of new policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Explore the models, data, and runtime behind Cosmos-H-Dreams:

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a new environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

This is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

Assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the new closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

The progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really shows how challenging this field is. 👏

It’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱

Looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨

#10046. Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image

The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong.

This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data.

The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica.

Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape.

Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error.

To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today.

In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said.

He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image.

"Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said.

Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®

#10044. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

Extract text and tables from document images

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

#10043. Lock your GitHub Actions

GitHub Actions now supports workflow lockfiles.

Because GitHub Actions are fetched from Git, the previous advice was to pin to a full SHA instead of a tag. This is because tags are mutable and susceptible to supply-chain attacks where an attacker points a previously safe tag at malicious code.

Install the gh-actions-lock extension to the gh CLI:

The workflow now uses vX.Y.Z tags and looks like this:

And it generates a lockfile at .github/workflows/actions.lock:

Commit modified workflows and the new lockfile.

Good news, both already support lockfiles! Your periodic updates will also update the lockfile. Remember to use cooldowns.

GitHub also recommends verifying lockfiles in CI to ensure it’s up-to-date and not corrupt.

They suggest copying this verify-lockfile.yml into your repo. I decided to put it into my existing lint workflow, but in its own job so it runs independently and in parallel:

Note I’m using the lightweight ubuntu-slim runner here. Also, it’s pinning to v0.4.1; we’ll have to update that at some point or figure out a way to automate it. That’s for another time.

Don’t forget that we just modified the actions in a workflow, so need to relock with gh actions-lock. Nothing actually changes if adding to lint.yml because it’s already locking actions/checkout. But if you created a new file like verify-lockfile.yml, you’ll need to relock for that. The CI will let you know.

zizmor is a security linter for GitHub Actions and strongly recommended. If you don’t use it, please do.

Versions before v1.32.0 tell you to hash-pin actions, and v1.32.0 is the first to support lockfiles.

#10042. US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity

Operators face longer connection waits and a growing need to bring their own electricity

Datacenter power consumption in the US is growing roughly ten times faster than grid capacity, meaning facilities may soon need to find a large chunk of their own electricity from other sources.

Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed.

Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing.

Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade.

Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period.

Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase.

Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster, as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030.

This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters.

Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies.

For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue.

"Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam.

"As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need."

Howden's business is insurance, and so Adam also notes that on-site generation introduces new operational and financial exposures, as operators take greater responsibility for their power infrastructure. ®

#10040. Russian cloud Yandex says drone attacks on its datacenters caused data loss

Now enables backup by default and hints a little on-prem infra never hurt anyone

Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters.

The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services.

On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.”

It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data.

Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud.

That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups.

Given that drones damaged three Yandex locations, and the war with Ukraine continues, users have good reasons to consider alternatives to its services.

Indeed, Yandex’s announcement of its recovery efforts links to a page extolling the virtues of a hybrid cloud when devising data protection strategies. That page also mentions Yandex’s own Stackland product, which brings its stack on-prem, as an example of a hybrid approach.

On Wednesday the company also launched a new availability zone named ru-central1-f. Yandex didn’t say where it’s located, other than to say it’s in “a new location.” Interestingly, Yandex has imposed quotas that limit the amount of resources users can access in the new availability zone and says it can’t yet handle traffic to private endpoints at the new facility.

Many nations have imposed sanctions that restrict sales of technology products to Russia. It’s therefore unsurprising that Yandex might struggle to provision enough infrastructure to allow untrammeled access to a new availability zone. ®

#10039. Let’s Write a PostScript Interpreter

I think the most trustworthy programming languages are those which are human-scale: languages which a single user could reasonably write from scratch on some readily-available computational substrate. Knowing how to make your own tools provides a satisfying feeling of power.

Today I’d like to take you on a brisk journey through the process of implementing an interesting subset of the PostScript programming language. We will ignore or simplify many features of the language, and we will elide most error-handling for simplicity, but every PostScript example we discuss will be a well-formed PostScript program which has the same behavior in our toy subset and a standard PostScript interpreter like Ghostscript.

PostScript is primarily designed for describing printed documents: it has a rich vocabulary of features for creating and manipulating raster and vector graphics. For the purposes of this article I will narrowly focus on its mechanics as a general-purpose programming language.

PostScript programs are composed of a series of whitespace-delimited tokens, plus a few special characters (% / ( ) < > [ ] { }) which immediately terminate the preceding token and begin a new one. The % character begins a line-comment. The / character can prefix a literal name, which we’ll discuss in more detail momentarily. The ( ) and < > characters enclose PostScript strings, which we will omit from our interpreter for simplicity. The [, ], { and } characters are used to enclose PostScript arrays and procedures, respectively, but are ordinary self-delimiting tokens. Given a PostScript program fragment:

The PostScript execution model centers around several stacks: chiefly, an operand stack which is used to pass arguments between operators and a dictionary stack which is used to associate names with values.

The above program fragment is executed as follows:

It’s also worth taking a moment to touch on PostScript arrays. The [ operator pushes a special value called mark onto the operand stack, and the ] operator pops all of the values of the operand stack down to the topmost mark and builds an array from them:

We’ll discuss programming in PostScript in more detail later, but this is enough to get building.

Our PostScript interpreter will be written in a very concise style of JavaScript that is influenced by the philosophy of Forth, an influential ancestor of PostScript:

Here are a few routines which illustrate this style:

If you’re finding yourself struggling to “skim” code in this style, try to slow down and read each definition carefully, character-by-character. You may also find it useful to experiment with each definition in your browser’s JavaScript console as you go along.

The first step in writing any interpreter is determining how we’ll represent data, in this case describing PostScript datatypes in terms of JavaScript datatypes:

Using primitive JavaScript values to represent most of these types will be particularly helpful for writing the definitions of all the operators.

Here are a set of definitions for constructing, accessing, and identifying various PostScript values:

Next, we need to translate PostScript syntax into the above data representations. We can use a JavaScript RegExp to split an input program into a sequence of tokens- line-comments (which can be discarded), special delimiters ([]{}), names, and numbers (which can be coerced into JavaScript numbers). While it is possible to implement { and } as PostScript operators, it is simpler for our purposes to cluster the tokens of procedures together as we parse the program:

The parse(x) routine will break it down into

The PostScript operand stack and dictionary stack can be represented as simple JavaScript global arrays- o and d, respectively:

Some simple routines for manipulating these stacks:

Executing pre-tokenized PostScript programs is very simple: we execute each token in sequence. Names are looked up in the dictionary stack and the corresponding operator or procedure is called; anything else is pushed onto the operand stack. Since operators are JavaScript functions, when we execute them we’ll pop a number of values from the operand stack corresponding to their argument list count and apply() them to the function. If the function returns something other than undefined, we’ll push the result onto the stack:

The large bulk of the machinery of our interpreter lives in the primitive operator definitions, but each is individually fairly simple, with the possible exception of the for operator, which needs a few helper routines for generating stepped ranges. Many of these operators are pure JavaScript functions which do not directly access or modify either stack and can be tested and understood in isolation.

To access the primitives from within exec() and execproc() we need to install them into the dictionary stack. Here’s a procedure to initialize both stacks:

We can now execute programs and observe their effects on the stacks:

For interactive use, we can wire everything up into a Read-Eval-Print-Loop (REPL). We’ll need at least some rudimentary output capabilities, so for starters we can install an extra primitive == which pops a value from the stack and displays it:

If we’re using Node.js we have to write our REPL in an event-driven style:

If we’re using QuickJS we can write a more straightforward infinite loop instead:

Either way, we now have a fancy PostScript-style desk calculator:

The entire interpreter in one piece, for reference.

Our interpreter offers a very small subset of the primitive operators supplied with standard PostScript. There are some fun finger-exercises to be had in fleshing out more of that set in terms of what we already have:

Try your hand at abs- compute the absolute value of a number:

How about min- find the minimum of two values on the stack?

It can also be worthwhile to try some classic functional programming exercises, like recursively computing the Fibonacci sequence:

There are, of course, more idiomatic iterative approaches:

I quite enjoy the way that enclosing PostScript expressions in [] acts like a more composable alternative to list comprehensions.

Here’s a utility routine for making a copy of an array with the elements in reversed order:

How many approaches can you think of for concatenating a pair of arrays, given the primitive operators we have at hand?

Much of my experience with concatenative programming languages like PostScript is with Forth, which uses slightly different names and factorings for most operators. Fortunately, PostScript is fairly malleable:

PostScript’s roll and index operators make it easier to reach deep into the stack than the usual Forth stack-twiddlers, but this also demands the programmer retain a larger perspective of the contents of the stack in their limited working memory as they read. Even rot/-rot can be controversial “code smells” to some Forthwrights.

In Forth, we can freely manipulate the “return stack” as well as the operand stack, usually with words like r> and >r for transferring values from the top of one stack to the other. Forth control structures will often store things like loop indices on the return stack between iterations in order to prevent them from interfering with the flow of arguments within the loop body. It can also be handy for temporarily stashing intermediate results to keep the operand stack shallow. PostScript has an “execution stack” for nested procedure bookkeeping, but it is not under direct control of the programmer; as a result we can’t use these sorts of idioms.

The dictionary stack offers nestable scopes for named local variables:

It’s even possible to build tidy abstractions around this pattern:

But since this approach produces dynamic rather than lexical scopes, it is not transparent to procedures we exec. Without an auxiliary stack to “hide” intermediate state, it can be surprisingly challenging to write higher-order functions. Try defining the equivalent of a Lispy (cond) conditional in PostScript and you’ll see what I mean:

PostScript has a tantalyzing bind operator (not implemented in our interpreter) which is meant to help sidestep the footguns of dynamic scope by eagerly replacing references to operators within a procedure with their values at bind-time. However, since bind concerns itself only with resolving operators, it isn’t useful for simulating general-purpose lexical scope; we’d need to build a more general mechanism for performing named substitutions within procedures.

My preceding semantic quibbles aside, I think PostScript is quite elegant, and well worth learning. Now that we have an interpreter for the language which fits on a printed page or two, we have an inviting foundation for experimentation. I’m sure that over the course of our brief explorations you’ve already thought of many new primitive operators you could add- sin, cos, pi, perhaps more tools for manipulating data like type, cvx, and cvlit, or a richer set of input and output routines?

You might find it worth the added bulk to add more robust error-handing. For example, you could make load tolerate undefined names and return a placeholder:

You could also implement a more complete range of datatypes and syntax, like (strings), non-integer numbers, and the <> syntax for dictionary “literals”.

Take your budding new human-scale programming environment in whatever direction you like. Enjoy the feeling of power.

#10038. Meta is back with Muse Glimmer: local, agentic, multimodal, and open source

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 support in transformers, both for the main model and the speculative decoding drafter. You can use AutoModelForMultimodalLM and AutoProcessor classes to load the model and the processor.

The same snippet runs unchanged on NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (ROCm) and Intel (XPU) GPUs, device_map="auto" places the model on whichever accelerator is available.

After loading the model, you can do text-only inference with it as follows.

We would need torchvision to be able to use images and text.

Muse Glimmer accepts images as input, as demonstrated here:

To work with videos we recommend installing torchcodec into the environment.

Muse Glimmer can answer complex questions about videos without audio. You can do video inference as follows, here’s an example from VideoMME2, which is the most popular video question answering benchmark.
