Here is an end to end script to perform object detection GitHub Gist

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 llama.cpp support. Meta has distributed calibrated quants in this repo, and Unsloth is releasing optimized quants as well. DFlash speculative decoding is supported as well. You can use a pre-built llama binary to start a llama server or a CLI. To install llama.cpp, run:

Then you can start the server as follows.

Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:8080 to chat with the built-in WebUI.

You can also query the server as follows.

You can also use llama server with coding agents like Pi.

DFlash uses a lightweight block-diffusion drafter model to provide same output with extra speed-ups in decoding phase. Transformers and llama.cpp ship support for DFlash drafter of Muse Glimmer day-0.

Below you can see how speculative decoding can speed-up generation in realistic setups. The video shows llama.cpp webui with DFlash on the left and regular generation on the right.

You can load the drafter and model as follows, and infer like how you would with base model with an additional parameter (shown in the upcoming snippets).

You can start llama server using following command. --spec-draft-n-max argument controls how many future tokens DFlash proposes during each speculative-decoding step. Muse Glimmer’s DFlash model was trained with a block size of 16, one anchor token plus 15 proposed tokens, so any value above 15 will be clamped to 15.

You can also use llama cli with speculative decoding drafter as follows.

For a managed, autoscaling deployment, open the Muse Glimmer 30B Inference Endpoints preset. The model is already selected: choose the organization, cloud provider, region, compatible GPU instance, authentication, and autoscaling settings, then review the hourly price and click Create Endpoint. Once its status is Running, you can test it in the Playground and copy the endpoint URL and model name from the Overview.

The deployed model exposes an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. Keep your Hugging Face token in an environment variable, set HF_ENDPOINT_URL to the URL shown in the Overview without /v1, and set HF_ENDPOINT_MODEL to the endpoint's model name.

See the Inference Endpoints documentation for configuration, autoscaling, security, logs, and monitoring.

For this release, we ship support for vLLM with transformers backend.

You can use TRL to fine-tune Muse Glimmer using various methods from SFT to Async GRPO. We have run two experiments on bf16 with Hopper-class GPUs with 80GB VRAM each.

As part of this release, we ship an example to fine-tune Muse Glimmer on small split of MolmoWeb dataset. This shows how to make model generate structured outputs and how to fine-tune on images.

We also experimented with running the model on OpenCode with AsyncGRPO example. Model shows strong coding capabilities, so we encourage you to try training with coding environments in OpenEnv and TRL.

Here are some fun ways to try out Muse Glimmer. In our opinion, the coolest thing about this model is that it is a local scale personal assistant that can code. That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! Let’s go team local 🚀

Assume the Inference Endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible /v1 API.

Set HF_TOKEN in the OpenClaw gateway environment, then add this to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Use the exact model ID returned by the endpoint’s /v1/models response if it differs.

If we hook up Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face MCP and update its AGENTS.md we give it the capability to find a quantized version of itself on the hub and run locally. This is handy if you want to work on something private, or just cut costs.

If you do this a second time, Muse Glimmer will find the cached weights and switch to them, so feel free to add a convenient command like /spawn.

Muse Glimmer inspects the machine and Hub, selects or creates a Q4_K_M GGUF, launches llama-server, and validates model discovery and chat completion. The result is a smaller local build behind an OpenAI-compatible API. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md.

https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/muse-glimmer-assets/resolve/Muse%20Glimmer%20Quantisation%20Demo%20-%20explained.mp4?download=true

By adding this to AGENTS.md openclaw or hermes will be able to solve the rest.

Muse Glimmer can also take care of the opposite. Let’s get Glimmer to deploy itself on Hugging Face Inference Endpoints. Which is useful if you want to speed up on some cutting edge hardware.

N.B. You can also just deploy Muse Glimmer to Inference Endpoints directly and connect your agent.

Muse Glimmer pins the model revision, deploys it to a protected Hugging Face Inference Endpoint, and verifies health, model discovery, and chat completion. It then connects the Claw agent with secrets and rollback preserved. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md. Muse glimmer will also need the Hugging Face MCP and/or the Hugging Face CLI and Skills.

Finally, let’s get Muse Glimmer to do some light RSI. We can instruct our agent to optimize its own inference engine for specific hardware, in this case a Nvidia H100. To do this, the agent will need to use another inference engine, like Inference Endpoints above.

Muse Glimmer benchmarks its own single-H100 serving stack, testing one reversible change at a time while holding the workload fixed. It keeps only correctness-passing gains and finishes with the fastest reproducible configuration. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md. Muse glimmer need the Hugging Face MCP and the Hugging Face CLI and Skills.

https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/muse-glimmer-assets/resolve/onyx-optimization-progress.gif?download=true

Try Muse Glimmer as a Hugging Face research agent. The Gradio Space sends each model request to a private Hugging Face Inference Endpoint through its OpenAI-compatible API. It also connects to the official Hugging Face MCP server, giving the agent read-only tools to search and inspect Hub repositories, models, datasets, Spaces, documentation, and papers.

We are happy to welcome Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face Hub. Try Muse Glimmer with your local coding setups today!

Timing is a bit suspicious Meta faced about $1B in fines over child-safety failures specifically a New Mexico judge found its platforms were harming children and that Meta didn’t warn the public about the dangers. now it’s releasing a cheaper API so others pay the fines, damage control.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

The day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏

InfoQ Homepage News Angular's TypeScript 7-Powered Compiler Enters Beta with Rust-Based Preprocessor

Nov 11, 2026 2 min read

The Angular team has shared details of a new version of its compiler, the Angular Preprocessor (ngp), which rewrites the analysis stage of the toolchain in Rust to clear the way for TypeScript 7 adoption. Alex Rickabaugh and Mark Techson announced the work on the Angular team blog in late September, shortly after Microsoft shipped TypeScript 7.0, whose Go-based rewrite removed the ts.Transformer API that Angular's ahead-of-time compiler depends on.

The existing compiler, ngc, wraps tsc and uses the Transformer API to turn decorators such as @Component and @Pipe into runtime instructions. The Go port offers no cross-language equivalent, and crossing the JS/Go boundary at every file would be prohibitive. The Angular team's answer is to decouple compilation from TypeScript's APIs and rebuild it on Oxc, the VoidZero Rust toolchain already powering Vite. The team pointed to the plan on X, framing it as a partial rewrite rather than a fresh start.

ngp runs in three stages. A Rust frontend using Oxc analyses files in parallel to discover Angular declarations and resolve metadata. The existing TypeScript template compiler then emits two artefacts, a runtime file containing the transformed component and a .ngtypecheck.ts file holding the Type Check Block (TCB) for template type-checking. Finally a downstream tool, whether tsgo, tsrs, esbuild or Rolldown, handles type-checking and JavaScript emission independently.

The bulk of ngp landed on 8 October in a single commit of more than 370,000 lines, around 56,000 of them Rust. Cédric Exbrayat of Ninja Squad benchmarked the beta against three projects ranging from 15 to 1,714 components and measured a 2x to 3x speedup on cold builds, with memory use on the largest project falling from 2.8 GB to 1.4 GB. Pairing ngp with tsrs and Rolldown gave the fastest pipeline, with tsgo and esbuild only marginally slower. They concluded there is further gains to be made:

This is already very promising, and there are certainly further gains to be made when the team focuses on performance optimization.

Christopher Holder at push-based.io took a different tack, writing vite-plugin-ngp to compile Angular files on demand. On the Super Productivity codebase (252 components), the dev server reached the first page in 10.5 seconds against 17.4 for ng serve, with template edits applying in 112 milliseconds rather than a 2.6 second full reload. On a generated 5,000-component app the gap widened to 1.6 seconds against 28.4. Holder cautioned that the plugin "is a prototype on a prototype" pinned to 22.3.0-next.2.

On Reddit, a number of developers are excited about the update and write up, with one commenting:

Read the whole article. Impressive. The Angular team surpassed my expectations!

VoidZero's own experimental Oxc Angular compiler, covered by InfoQ in April, reported a roughly 97% improvement on narrower workloads but is now described as "actively seeking maintainers". The Angular team confirmed VoidZero's work influenced the architecture and that the two groups have been collaborating, with ngp becoming the official path.

Teams on earlier Angular versions should first run the standard update guide to reach v20 or later. Adoption of ngp is expected to land in a minor release of Angular 22 once TypeScript 7.1 restores the compiler API; until then production builds should stay on ngc.

Angular is Google's open-source, TypeScript-first web framework, widely adopted across enterprise applications and built around standalone components and signal-based reactivity.

#10035. Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates

Couldn’t get the hardware it needed to generate certs, so tried to code a workaround

Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates.

The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.”

eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.”

The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four.

Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.”

eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA.

It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A.

Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May.

The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created.

The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra.

The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment.

Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.”

#10034. Secure Exclaves and Ambient Sensing

While ambient sensing relies on processing input from the camera or microphone, it must never record audio or video, nor expose it to the rest of the operating system. Instead, it must reduce the sensor stream to far simpler signals, such as whether a specific sound was detected or whether an enrolled userâs face or voice was recognized, while protecting the raw sensor data during processing and discarding it once complete.

To accomplish this, we have created Secure Exclaves: protected and compartmentalized runtimes used to process camera and microphone data separately from the rest of the system. Isolation features added across many core components of the silicon work in tandem to protect Secure Exclaves and keep them segregated from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in a Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.

We use Secure Exclaves to protect entirely new use cases, like person recognition on HomeView as well as Siri Recap and Live Rewind, as described here. We also use them to protect the on-screen camera and microphone indicators used in iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, as well as the camera indicators in MacBook Neo and HomeView, improving security for our users across the board.

To protect ambient sensing, we aimed to build a system that operated in two distinct modes: ambient mode and active mode, for both camera and microphone. In ambient mode, a sensor can respond to particular triggers in the world around it, but only specific metadata may be shared with the rest of the system. In active mode, full sensor data can be released to the main operating system (OS), and a secure indicator reliably informs the user that itâs happening.

Meeting this challenge ultimately required building a new, isolated computing environment that could handle the full performance demands of ambient sensing use cases, yet stay cleanly separated from the main OS with three primary requirements:

Building a new secure runtime requires a highly secure OS foundation. For this reason, we utilized an Apple-customized version of the L4 microkernel which we originally built for some of our most security-sensitive deployments, including the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP). This microkernel uses capabilities, which are secure resource handles that both identify and authorize access to the underlying resource. This simple but powerful mechanism is applied to both memory isolation and IPC security, enabling us to build a secure system that contains no extraneous authority. The exclaves microkernel, and our approach to formal verification of its correctness, are described in detail later in this post.

Secure Exclaves run in a different processor execution context from the main OS, which allows us to employ an independent operating system specially designed to handle high-security, high-performance workloads. But isolation also requires careful handling of all shared resources available to the application processor: most importantly, system memory and communication with coprocessors.

Isolating memory for the exclusive use of Secure Exclaves presented a serious engineering challenge: management of the page tables, which organize and protect main device memory, is usually handled by the main OS. We laid the groundwork for isolation in earlier releases, by carving out and rebuilding this subsystem as the Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM): a standalone component that handles page table and memory logic, and runs at a higher privilege level than the main OS kernel. It doesnât share data or code with the main OS, and is separately loaded by the boot loader. This rearchitecture not only hardened the entire system against certain kernel-level attacks, but also created the foundation for isolating Secure Exclave memory.

SPTM relies on Apple silicon primitives to protect the memory used by exclaves from the rest of the system. It manages every physical page of memory used by the application processor, and enforces that software executing in Secure Exclaves have a separate and isolated view of memory than that seen by the main OS. Microkernel capabilities are used to control memory permissions of every individual exclave. This allows each exclave to access only its own memory, providing an additional layer of protection.

Next, Secure Exclaves must account for the other coprocessors and sensors connected to the Apple silicon fabric. Where a coprocessor is essential to secure sensing, such as our Always-On Processor (AOP), a secure compartment within that coprocessorâs operating system handles the processing needed for communication with Secure Exclaves. The coprocessor secure compartment is also built on top of the exclaves microkernel, maintaining security assurance continuity across the application processor and coprocessors. Other resources like sensor memory are protected with specialized memory filters, placed between each resource and the shared fabric, which can only be configured by the SPTM. This propagates the memory isolation property throughout the system.

Some of the secure sensing workloads that run in Secure Exclaves need access to high-performance inference hardware to run demanding machine learning models. To enable this, we extended the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) by adding isolated workload queues, like those we use in the SEP. Memory filters protect those queues from being modified or accessed by the main OS, and switching from an isolated to a standard queue flushes any local storage to prevent information leaks. With these changes, we can offer high-performance inference to power intelligent ambient sensing.

Altogether, the computational, memory, and peripheral isolation technologies stack together to create an isolated but high-performance execution context. Within this context, we can place a specialized, secure operating system with microphone and camera access, running with the full power of Apple silicon.

To handle ambient sensing tasks, Secure Exclaves must be able to exchange small amounts of metadata with the main OS. Traditional inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms are designed for maximum flexibility, providing open-ended interfaces that can be composed with arbitrary complexity when moving data. For Secure Exclaves, we approached the problem from the opposite angle, and set out to design IPC primitives that could enable tightly restricted, completely predictable communication.

To do so, we built a new communication mechanism called Secure IPC, written in Swift for memory safety. It combines an interface description language with a runtime that securely connects the components that are allowed to communicate. All exclaves use Secure IPC to communicate with each other and with the main OS. This design prevents unanticipated crosstalk between components and ensures that only authorized information can flow across IPC boundaries. Each Secure IPC interface from an exclave to the main OS is rigorously audited to ensure that only the minimal metadata needed to run an ambient sensing use case can leave the exclave.

Microkernel capabilities are used to control the IPC connections of every exclave. By default, exclaves are unable to communicate or even refer to one another. An exclave may only initiate IPC if it has an explicit capability to an IPC connection. Therefore, Secure Exclaves have complete control over every IPC interface and connection in the system. The combination of the exclaves microkernel and Secure IPC makes Secure Exclaves the most secure runtime Apple has ever created, and weâve put it at the heart of how we secure ambient sensing.

When moving from ambient sensing to a full, active sensor use case, such as a conversation with Siri or a FaceTime video session, the system must communicate to the user that it is now sharing broad access to the sensor with the app that has requested it. We build on our existing visual language to communicate this â either an LED, or an indicator dot drawn on the display â but back it with a novel, high level of security thatâs without industry precedent.

A specialized exclave, called the Exclave Indicator Controller, is the overall system gatekeeper for sensor data. It only allows data to flow after establishing that the indicator is activated, and has been visible for a sufficient amount of time. Since multiple apps can request audio and video data simultaneously, the Indicator Controller deconflicts these requests and makes sure the appropriate indicator appears.

For products like HomeView that use an LED, just the Exclave Indicator Controller is needed. It can toggle the LED directly and ensure that it is bright enough to be visible.

For products like iPhone that use an indicator dot on the screen, an additional exclave works to ensure that the dot is visible whenever the system is sharing full sensor data. This display exclave uses a specialized hardware block in the display subsystem to check what pixels have been drawn to the screen. This enforcement provides affordances for various operating system modes, like Night Shift, that can affect the appearance of the indicator dot. It also ensures that the pixels meet a minimum brightness threshold and are not obscured by nearby pixels. Trusted firmware in the display controller shares precise backlight values with the exclave, ensuring the indicator is truly visible to the user.

Together with the isolation and controlled interface components of Secure Exclaves, this system provides an incredibly powerful mechanism for securely processing high-sensitivity workloads.

To illustrate how these components work together, we describe the person recognition flow using the camera on HomeView â an ambient sensing use case protected by Secure Exclaves. HomeView must passively perform minimal visual processing at all times to detect whether a person is in the field of view, but this must not make camera data available to the broader system. The Secure Exclaves system allows person recognition to occur quickly and accurately, while keeping the ambient visual data protected within exclaves. This means HomeView can recognize who is using it, react to nearby movement, and display content based on whether a user is nearby or far away.

At startup, the person recognition exclave loads previously enrolled face and voice recognition models and the identity database from the secure storage exclave (1).

A continuous stream of camera frames is passed to the camera exclave, which detects faces, applies a bounding box, and queues the frames for further processing (2). The camera exclave informs daemons in the main OS that a person may be present; however, no image data leaves the Secure Exclaves (3).

At the same time, microphone audio data is processed through the audio exclaves for anomaly detection and echo cancellation, before being passed to the person recognition exclave (4). As above, the exclaves inform daemons in the main OS that someone may be present, without sharing audio data (5).

Next, the person recognition exclave requests that the Neural Engine exclave load the face and voice print models to produce face and voice prints (6). All data remains in exclave-controlled memory at all times and is not accessible by the main OS. To achieve this, the Neural Engine uses isolated work queues that are dedicated to exclaves, ensuring that the state of the Neural Engine is cleared after each model completes.

Finally, the orchestration service within the person recognition exclave matches the resulting prints against the identity database of enrolled users, and combines the face and voice identification to produce a confidence score. Only this metadata â person identifier, position, and confidence level â is returned to the person recognition daemon running in the main OS (7). The system integrates the outputs so that they are properly reflected in features that depend on user identity, such as Calendar, Messages, Apple Music, or compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone (8). No audio or video data is shared with the operating system as this recognition process is performed.

We also describe the âHey Siriâ flow on the latest iPhone models to show how this new architecture can improve security for existing use cases. A phone must passively perform minimal audio processing at all times to detect when a user has said the wake words for Siri. The Secure Exclaves system allows the âHey Siriâ flow to occur quickly and accurately, while keeping the ambient audio protected within exclaves until an active Siri session begins.

The flow begins with the Always-On Processor (AOP), a low-power coprocessor that continuously monitors for wake-word utterances (1). If the rough first-pass filter on the AOP detects a potential âHey Siri,â it wakes up the main processor and passes the audio buffer to the audio exclave (2). This exclave performs an echo cancellation pass to make the audio more intelligible, and then passes the audio to the Siri exclave (3).

Now the Siri exclave runs a second pass on the audio to confirm whether wake words were in fact said (4). This model is larger and more finely tuned â running on the main processor lets it filter out significantly more false positives than the AOP can do on its own.

If this second pass confirms the wake-word detection, the Siri exclave notifies the Siri daemon running in the main OS (5). No audio is shared with the daemon at this point: just the flag that it should wake up. The Siri daemon then begins an active session by requesting microphone access from the audio driver (6). The driver calls into the UI to draw a microphone indicator (7), then asks for audio access from the Exclave Indicator Controller (EIC) (8).

The EIC asks the secure display exclave to check that the pixels rendered to the display â including their colors, shape, and display duration â all match whatâs expected for a microphone indicator (9). If that check passes, the system transitions from ambient mode to active mode. The EIC permits the audio transfer (10), and the Siri exclave sends its daemon the historical audio that includes âHey Siriâ along with the rest of the request (11). The EIC ensures that the indicator stays on screen until the Siri daemon ends the audio session, with a minimum duration of three seconds.

This section takes a closer look at the underpinnings of Secure Exclaves for those readers who have particular interest in the technical details of the systemâs implementation.

Microkernels allow large, secure systems to be constructed by minimizing the trusted computing base (TCB), which is the set of code that must be trusted to maintain system security. Unlike traditional kernels, such as XNU or Linux, which handle hardware, networking, and resource management in the kernel, the exclaves microkernel implements only the absolute minimum functionality required to run and isolate application services.

While the exclaves microkernel was developed from scratch at Apple, its design is guided by modern microkernel research. It is a capability-based kernel, like seL4 or keyKOS, meaning that system components have no permissions by default. Instead, components may only interact with other components or hardware if explicitly granted a capability to do so.

Because the exclaves microkernel has such a small TCB, Apple has been able to incrementally apply formal verification, using mathematical proofs to verify that the kernel's C implementation behaves exactly as defined by a high-level functional specification. This rigorous process has proven highly effective at discovering and eliminating subtle, critical logic bugs in core subsystems that could have otherwise led to kernel compromise: incomplete input validation of syscalls, inconsistent state updates, misaligned reads, and malformed page-table updates. It has also eliminated some classes of C undefined behavior.

To integrate with the existing operating system, the microkernel implements a user-level scheduling model inspired by the Composite component-based OS. In this model, the microkernel relies on XNU to donate CPU execution time. When XNU calls into the microkernel, the user-level scheduler executes the appropriate threads. When a thread completes, a timer tick occurs, or an interrupt fires, control is handed back to XNU, which can then call back into the microkernel to resume execution.

Building Secure Exclaves on top of the exclaves microkernel lets complex system services run as isolated user-level tasks. This architecture ensures that these components operate with strong isolation from each other and from the rest of the system, preventing a compromise in one service from affecting the others.

Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to demonstrate that a system satisfies specific properties that we define. At Apple, we've performed extensive formal verification in silicon development for over 15 years, and in 2019 we began using formal verification to prove classical cryptography, including the hardware Public Key Accelerator (PKA) â the part of Apple silicon that performs elliptic-curve public-key operations. More recently, corecrypto, Apple's cryptographic library, gained implementations of the quantum-secure ML-KEM and ML-DSA algorithms. These implementations have been formally verified to ensure that they are faithful to the FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 specifications.

For the exclaves microkernel â the centerpiece in the security of exclave-based systems â we draw on the same internal expertise to formally verify that our C implementation satisfies an abstract functional specification: a precise, mathematical description of what the code should do. This provides a significantly greater degree of assurance than conventional software testing allows; in theory, it gives us strong confidence that our implementation behaves exactly as specified wherever the proof applies. The practical considerations are more complicated. Regardless of how it is applied, formal verification requires a tremendous investment of time and deep expertise. The implementation and its specification must be represented with carefully chosen mathematical formulas. To draw correct conclusions, the formulas must faithfully model the relevant behaviors of both the implementation and the specification, and be structured so as to enable the proof to be written in simple steps.

Since the exclaves microkernel is actively developed and frequently changing, our formal verification efforts serve primarily as a tool to discover deep logic problems â for example, incomplete input validation of syscalls, inconsistent state updates, misaligned reads, and malformed page-table updates. As a side effect, we also show the absence of some classes of C undefined behavior for the code we formally verify. While other methods, such as testing and fuzzing, are useful for identifying bugs in the implementation and are often the first line of defense, formal verification has been able to discover subtle but critical problems in many of the kernel's subsystems, with the potential for full kernel compromise â for example, in the recursive algorithm used to free a capability storage object (CNode), in the implementation of sending capabilities over inter-process communication (IPC), and in execution-context (EC) state management when running on a multiprocessor (SMP) system. Thanks to close collaboration between the kernel engineers and the formal verification engineers, many of these issues have been discovered at early stages of development. Because of these constant changes, we do not claim complete coverage of all aspects of the kernel; instead, formal verification is applied gradually and incrementally to different parts. To do this, we rely on Isabelle/HOL with AutoCorres2 to build a mathematical model of the kernel implementation from the C source code, against which we perform our formal verification.

exclaveOS builds on the exclaves microkernel to create an environment isolated from XNU and Darwin user space. Software with direct access to devices that capture sensitive personal information, such as cameras and microphones, is placed into exclaveOS along with software that manages access to exclaveOS. Drivers, daemons, and applications running in Darwin must call through the access management software in exclaveOS in order to gain access to these devices.

All of the software in XNU, Darwin user space, and exclaveOS executes on the application processor cores. When user-level code in Darwin or an in-kernel driver wishes to communicate with software in exclaveOS, it performs a remote procedure call (RPC). This call is passed via the XNU kernel to a specific unit of software on the exclaveOS side, which can then interact with the remainder of exclaveOS as part of handling the RPC.

Because each RPC is handled on behalf of code that was running on a thread in XNU, the code that handles the RPC in exclaveOS runs on the same XNU thread. This means that XNU is responsible for scheduling all code running in exclaveOS, which gives exclaveOS the benefits of all the optimization provided by the XNU scheduler. Whenever code is preempted or synchronizes in exclaveOS, the state of that code is captured by the microkernel; a user-level scheduler in exclaves provides XNU only enough information to synchronize related threads and to later resume execution.

Both Darwin and exclaveOS have small trusted elements that manage low-level access to resources, primarily by restricting what physical and device memory either side is permitted to directly map and access. The SPTM controls what XNU and Darwin user space are permitted to access and the exclaves microkernel controls what software in exclaveOS is permitted to access. These two components mutually trust each other to enforce the access restrictions that the other side relies on, forming the lowest-level boundary between the two sides and cooperatively managing execution on the shared processor cores.

Secure Exclaves have a file storage protocol that is designed to prevent unauthorized communication channels between XNU and exclaves, as well as between individual exclaves. File system access is not presumed â it is statically expressed in system configuration, and only granted to components that genuinely need it.

File access can be read-only, and there are also specialized, component-only read-write sections of the file system. All read-only files are checked against an integrity catalog that ships with the OS. All writable files are only readable by the exclave that wrote them, and all writes are encrypted.

To boot exclaves, iBoot places the exclaves microkernel and an initial static code bundle, along with an integrity catalog for the read-only parts of the file system, into wired memory. Signatures for dynamically loadable code are read and compared against the integrity catalog at boot. During runtime, to load dynamic components of the system, code is read from the read-only file system, and then validated against the in-memory signatures before being made executable. No code can execute that did not ship with Secure Exclaves.

exclaveOS is the operating system and runtime we use on top of the microkernel to run sensitive code. As a microkernel-based operating system, exclaveOS implements the majority of OS functionality as user-level servers, each with a minimal set of capabilities required to function. Significant portions of exclaveOS are written in Swift for built-in memory safety. The OS builds on several key concepts:

At boot, the exclaveOS root task runs, creates all of the ExclaveCore address spaces as described, and distributes the relevant kernel capabilities. Included in the distributed resources are communication endpoints to other address spaces. After boot, the root task is destroyed, and the ability to create new connections between address spaces is irreversibly removed from the running system.

The creation and destruction of ExclaveKit address spaces is not done by the root task. Instead, each conclave has an associated ExclaveCore called a conclave launcher. Each conclave launcher maintains a connection to XNU so that its corresponding daemon can invoke it to create the ExclaveKit address spaces in its conclave. If a daemon is terminated, XNU invokes that daemonâs conclave launcher to terminate the daemonâs ExclaveKit address spaces. Importantly, while a conclave launcher can create and destroy address spaces, it cannot create the connections between address spaces, but instead must use the existing connections that the root task gave it at boot.

Once the root task is destroyed, no remaining part of the system has such broad authority. For example, the root task gives the capability to manage physical memory to the physical memory server but restricts that capability such that memory mapped through it can only be mapped read-only or read-write. On the other hand, the capability to distribute read-execute (but not writable) access to physical memory is given to a code loading server. Every component in the system can request memory from the physical memory server, but only conclave launchers are connected to the code loading server.

exclaveOS puts a component architecture on top of the capability model that the exclaves microkernel provides. Communication between these components is handled by Secure IPC.

Secure IPC is a system for describing software components and the interfaces they provide, and managing their behavior at runtime. All communication between components, as well as into and out of exclaveOS, is handled by Secure IPC. Component interfaces are described ahead of time in a type-safe description language, allowing RPC data flow around the system to be audited and approved before itâs ever run.

Secure IPC is used to describe the interface for all software in exclaveOS, allowing for the movement of all RPC data to be audited and understood at build time. At runtime, the system description is used by the root task to hand the components for each address space only the capabilities they need to construct their pre-approved RPC links. This strict build-time declaration of interfaces as well as the one-time construction of RPC links at runtime enables the static, type-safe transmission of data around the system.

The Secure IPC IDL is a Swift-like, type-safe language where interfaces are described using scalar values, structures, and enumerations. These are used to declare methods and the services they are a part of. Components tie everything together by implementing a set of services as well as declaring the services they themselves are clients of in their initializers.

The Secure IPC compiler takes these IDL files for each component and then generates the Swift and optionally C source code that provides a runtime interface for the software they describe. The generated implementation makes use of a single, audited set of encode and decode methods for each of the types used in the interface, completely centralizing the processing of arbitrary data in the system.

In exclaveOS, the initialization and management of software is completely handled by the operating system. At boot, the Secure IPC component runtime exists in each exclaveOS address space, and the root task hands it data generated at build time as well as runtime handles such as endpoint capabilities. Secure IPC passes this data to the component initializers that were constructed by the compiler to create their runtime instances. The runtime then handles notifying the component instances of new clients arriving or departing, for example an ExclaveCore component being told that a client in a conclave has launched or exited.

At the very lowest layer, Secure IPC interacts with the operating system itâs running on to move RPC data between instances of components and services. When communicating between components in exclaveOS, Secure IPC encodes a message into a microkernel IPC buffer and invokes the endpoint capability attached to the service. The same runtime is then also used to manage data transmission from a daemon running in Darwin user space to its conclave running in exclaveOS, in which case it encodes into a buffer that it hands to XNU with a system call.

The SPTM is a highly privileged piece of software that defines and enforces the security policies that govern page table management for the kernel, user applications, and coprocessors. Its intent is to protect the overall system by securing the page tables against attackers without trusting the kernel. On SPTM-protected products, the kernel cannot write a page table entry itself. Every mapping change is a request to the SPTM, which validates it against policy before applying it.

In order to enforce security policies at this level, the SPTM must necessarily own all of the architectural state that pertains to CPU and IOMMU page table management. This covers the page tables themselves, the data and code that manage them, and the VMSA (Virtual Memory System Architecture) registers and IOMMU translation control registers. The SPTM achieves this by placing itself in a separate, more privileged execution mode that the hardware isolates from the kernel, and by protecting all of the memory that backs page tables and ancillary data structures such that even the kernel itself cannot modify them.

The SPTM governs every page of DRAM exposed to the application processor using a powerful type system. Every page holds an associated type and may be retyped to another type subject to an allow-list of permitted transitions and security policy decisions. Pages mapped into a userspace process carry one type, while pages backing kernel private memory can carry a significantly more policy-constrained type that, for example, only ever permits a single kernel mapping of the page to exist.

This type system centrally enables the SPTM to define a given page type's owner, mapping permissions and policy that must apply when executing under each of the SPTM, XNU kernel, and Secure Exclave execution contexts. The result is a separate permission view for each context, enforced at the hardware level by Apple silicon.

The SPTM, coupled with Apple silicon security advancements, provides the foundation for modern secure memory management principles across our platforms. Under this design, Secure Exclave private memory is assigned types that only the Secure Exclave context owns. The OS kernel cannot retype these pages, and cannot map them into another CPU or IOMMU address space or otherwise have a path to read their contents. Even the SPTM itself, by design, keeps no mapping to this memory. This provides clean separation between kernel and Secure Exclave private memory resources.

We believe Secure Exclaves set a new standard for operating system security in the industry. This high-performance, high-assurance system can handle the most demanding workloads for ambient sensing, while providing an exceptional level of protection for the audio and visual data captured by device sensors. No security architecture is ever finished, and Secure Exclaves are no exception. And we are committed to continuing to harden this system, fueled by AI-accelerated vulnerability research and expanded formal verification coverage. As our products deliver increasingly intelligent features to our users, we see Secure Exclaves as a critical step in giving our users clarity and confidence about how their Apple products respond to the world around them.

#10033. Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:

The GIF below shows the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only shows up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

#10032. AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC

Hyperscale meets micro-computing by offering APIs to test your apps

AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC.

As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.”

The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs.

“You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use.

AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.”

The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub. The Register found over 1,300 items on that page.

While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud.

“It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.”

AWS publishes “fidelity scores” that detail how closely the emulator works on different AWS services. Amazon tries to achieve full fidelity, so the emulator produces the same results as AWS for valid API calls, and the same errors for invalid ones.

Coding agents can also drive the Emulator, an option The Register mentions because AWS advises the easiest way to check if a project will work with the tool is to use the aws-emulator skill for AI coding agents.

“With the skill, your agent finds the AWS operations and resources that your project depends on. It checks them against the fidelity tests and fidelity scores for the emulator. It then tells you which parts of your project you can rely on the emulator for, and which ones might behave differently from AWS,” according to AWS documentation.

AWS has made the emulator available as an RPM or Debian package. Mac and PC users will need to run Docker and an image of the Emulator.

“You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint,” Abib instructed. “When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.”

“From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment.”

The cloud colossus’s intent appears, as ever, to encourage more use of its cloud – in this case by satisfying developers their code will run well when deployed there, and making it easy for them to test for that. ®

#10031. Build Low-Latency Multilingual Voice Agents: Open Weights & Full Deployment Control with NVIDIA Magpie TTS

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new)

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

This release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:

Source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.

#10029. Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data

PARTNER CONTENT: Real-time endpoint data keeps AI-driven IT operations accurate, fast and under control

Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin?

Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse.

Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. Then teams had to work out which copies the internet could reach and check for signs of earlier attack. An inventory built from a periodic snapshot can't answer those questions on the day they matter.

The second is tool-hopping. Answering "where does this run, and can the internet reach it?" often means pivoting across an asset inventory, a vulnerability scanner and an external attack surface tool, each with its own view. Every hop adds delay. Every console is another chance to disagree with the last.

The third is pace. Several security firms reported exploitation attempts before PHP released its fixes, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. Frontier AI models helped find PHP2Shell, and in April Anthropic said its Claude Mythos Preview model had found thousands of previously unknown flaws across every major operating system and browser. With models like these in the picture, the old rhythm of disclose, patch and verify assumes a gap that keeps shrinking.

Put an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data and these problems don't go away. They scale.

Endpoints are where work happens and where many attacks end up, so they are the ground truth for any decision about the estate. Four qualities make that data a sound foundation for autonomous action:

Accuracy: Live data from the endpoints themselves, not a snapshot that was true last week.

Speed: A short path from question to action, with no hopping between tools to reconcile answers.

Control: Approvals and an audit trail, plus the ability to roll back, so any automated action can be reviewed and reversed.

Shared truth: IT operations, security and the system of record working from one view, rather than arguing over whose data is right.

Matt Psencik, a threat research engineer at Tanium, put the visibility problem bluntly when PHP2Shell broke: "The installations that worry me most are the ones a security team doesn't know it owns."

AI sits on both sides of this. It helped researchers find the PHP2Shell flaws, and attackers can use it to build exploits too. For defenders, AI works best as the operator and the interface: it takes a plain-language question, works out what to ask of the data, and proposes or carries out the next step. But it is only as good as the data it is grounded in. A fluent answer built on outdated information is still wrong, just more confidently so. Keeping people in the loop where stakes are high is what makes automation safe to expand.

Teams don't need to hand over the keys all at once. Start here:

Find every copy: Don't stop at the installed-applications list. PHP2Shell showed that software bundled inside other products can slip past it. Compare your CMDB against what is really on your network and record exact versions.

Draw the lines: Rank systems by what the internet can reach, then decide which response actions run automatically, which need approval and which are never delegated. Write it down before an agent needs it.

Pilot one low-risk workflow: Pick something contained, build approval into it, and read the audit trail before widening the scope.

Teams can also shorten the pilot with a partner. World Wide Technology (WWT), a Tanium partner, works with many large organizations on technology rollouts and hosts a Tanium lab in its Advanced Technology Center, where customers can test an approach hands-on before moving it into production.

That second problem, the hopping, is the one Tanium Atlas was built to close. Instead of moving between consoles, an operator asks a plain-language question, gets an answer from live endpoint data, and acts on it inside limits the team sets, with every action recorded. Want to see how it works in practice? Click here and set up time to see Tanium in action.

#10028. Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

Give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

We reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

So on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that shows up in the token bill.

Consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

Delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:

On the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:

Figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

The two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

We give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.)

Both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

The ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

DeepSeek-V3.2 — by difficulty (baseline → +memory): the two systems start from different no-memory baselines (79.8 vs 72.0 TGC overall) because of the prompt-template difference above.
